speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON NATIONAL CENOTAPH AND WORLD WAR II BOOK OF REMEMBRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce the policy of the government regarding the selection of a repository for the world war II Book of Remembrance and a site for the national cenotaph to honour Canada's youth who have given their lives in the cause of freedom. In my statement, which appears on page 2122 of Hansard of March 14, 1956, I informed hon. members that an advisory committee had been established to consider these matters and that the committee's report was receiving the attention of the government.
The government has accepted the unanimous recommendation of that committee and has decided that a national memorial, to honour our fallen of all conflicts and to house the world war II Book of Remembrance, shall be constructed on Nepean point in the city of Ottawa where an area shall also be provided for the erection of a national cenotaph and for the holding of national commemorative services. This memorial will take the form of a structure of a design appropriate to keep alive the remembrance of all those who have given their lives for Canada. The focal point within the memorial will be the Altar of Remembrance. The matter is now in the hands of my colleague, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), who is proceeding with the preliminary arrangements and planning for the construction of the memorial and the cenotaph.
Besides serving as a repository for the world war II Book of Remembrance, it is intended that the memorial shall also house a copy of the world war I book. It is not the intention to move the world war I Book of Remembrance from the memorial chamber in this building which, as hon. members know, in its decorative treatment, refers specifically to that conflict. However, relatives of the fallen and citizens at large who visit the national memorial in the future may wish also to see the world war I Book of Remembrance and it is thought appropriate that a copy should repose there.
The committee in its report considered the possibility of the preparation of books of
remembrance for those who lost their lives in other conflicts such as Korea and those previous to world war I.
The world war II Book of Remembrance will be completed in the autumn of 1956, and it was therefore necessary for the committee to consider a temporary repository for the book until such time as a permanent repository could be constructed. The government has accepted the committee's recommendation that the book be placed in the houses of parliament, and it has now been decided that a temporary base, on which the book will rest, shall be placed in the memorial chamber. This will have the advantage of having both books of remembrance in the same location until the national memorial is ready.
In its annual brief to the cabinet last November, the Canadian Legion recommended that a national cenotaph be erected and suggested that it be situated in the grounds in front of the peace tower. However, after much consideration, the advisory committee concluded that the most suitable location would be found in the area near the proposed national memorial where there would be ample space for national commemorative services, with parades of service personnel and veterans, and a large gathering of the public. I might say that it is not the intention to move the world war I national memorial from its position in Confederation square where it is perhaps the most conspicuous monument to meet the eye of the visitor approaching this capital city by the driveway from the south.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the very serious damage already caused in rural Manitoba as a result of the flooding of the Assiniboine river, will the government consider having steps taken to have the public works department do such dredging or other construction as may be necessary to prevent a recurrence of this condition, and also might I ask if the government has given any consideration to taking steps to see that those farmers and others who have suffered damage by reason of this flood will be compensated?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think we should take the initiative in seeking out claims for damages to be paid by the taxpayers of Canada generally to those who suffer from floods. There are some disasters that are of such magnitude that the public opinion of the nation is moved and it is felt that there should be some assistance given. But I think it would be quite a wrong attitude to take that the taxpayers of the nation generally are the insurers of each other against damages that do happen every year in very many places throughout the nation.
I have been receiving communications that would imply that there is a responsibility for any flooding from a stream that at any time was regarded as a navigable stream. Of course, where there are really navigable streams there are efforts made to keep them as free from obstructions as possible and to

do that which will minimize the possibility of floods. Now, with respect to the first part of the hon. gentleman's question he will remember that after the flood of 1950 there was a joint commission set up to examine the measures that might be taken to minimize the dangers of these floods, and a very intensive study was made of the situation. The costs of the measures suggested were indicated and some time ago the premier of Manitoba, to whose government the report had been submitted, wrote suggesting that we should take the initiative in setting up another commission to determine whether the economic value of the diminution of the danger would be anything like the cost of providing these works. We wrote back suggesting that our personnel was always ready to co-operate with them, but that was something the initiative for which should be taken by the government of Manitoba itself. I can assure the hon. gentleman that if there was any thought that by some dredging of the Assiniboine river these dangers could be overcome, that would be done at once.
I am not an engineer, but I understand that it would require very extensive engineering work to have any effect upon that area because there are floods that come from not only the Assiniboine but the tributaries to the Assiniboine, the Red river and also from the lakes into which these rivers flow. The whole matter is one of very serious concern to the people of that area and I am sure that the hon. gentleman was delighted, as we all were, to hear these reports that the weather we have been having over the last few days has diminished very substantially the fears that were entertained about the flood possibilities this year.
There have been some floods from the Assiniboine and from the LaSalle and I know that everything that can be done at this time is being done. As to the ultimate solution, it will require further studies before any conclusion can be reached because I understand that the Assiniboine now flows through dikes that are much higher than the level of the surrounding plains. These are matters of great concern, but there are these cycles. It is not so very long ago that there was concern expressed about the sufficiency of water, and now the concern is about the possibility of providing ways through which these abundant waters can reach the northern seas. The subject will have to receive further study. We cannot take the position that it is the responsibility of the federal government to take the initiative for these problems which arise in all of the ten Canadian provinces.
Inquiries of the Ministry
The hon. gentleman realizes, as I do, that there are still Canadian provinces and that they have jurisdiction over their local affairs, but there are matters which require the cooperative efforts of the federal government representing the taxpayers of the whole nation. The problems have to be studied and examined and recommended upon by the local authorities. Up to the present time I think the federal government has, whenever there has been a major disaster that was looked upon as such by the Canadian public generally, recommended to parliament such measures as were acceptable to the Canadian public generally.

My question was related to that. Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) asked me this question:
Has any consideration been given to amending the Canada Evidence Act so that microphotographic film would be taken as proof of records of municipal governments?
I do not think there is any great urgency to this question, so as the answer is rather lengthy I suggest that I be permitted to place it on the record.
Our files indicate that this question has been considered on at least three occasions upon the basis of representations by or on behalf of municipalities in Ontario. On each occasion we have refused the requests of the municipalities upon, amongst others, the following grounds:
1.	As I have already indicated, the Canada Evidence Act applies only to criminal prosecutions and proceedings in the Exchequer Court of Canada. It would therefore seem that an amendment along the lines proposed, to the Canada Evidence Act only, would be of little assistance to municipalities. For them, amendment of the provincial evidence act would seem to be more appropriate.

Whether under such a provincial amendment municipalities should be permitted to destroy documents and rely for evidence on photographic copies thereof is a decision which we think should be made by the provincial authorities which created the municipalities and clothed them with their present powers and responsibilities.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with the custom that has been established upon the presentation of this motion I am availing myself of this opportunity to bring up a subject which has assumed increasing importance throughout the whole of Canada. It has been discussed here before, it has been dealt with by many public bodies, but it assumes today a sense of urgency which calls for consideration here and in every part of this country. I am referring to the plight of the municipalities, caught as they are by the withdrawal of taxing powers and with the enormous increase in expenditures with which they are confronted.
We read constantly about the crisis in education. We read a great deal about the demands in the field of health. We read a great deal about the need for improvement in the general structure of our highway system throughout the country. We read a great deal about the need for modernization of our facilities for handling the highway traffic of this country. All these and other similar problems must be faced in varying degrees to an extent never before contemplated by the municipal governments of Canada.
Those municipal councils, whether they be urban councils or rural councils, must deal with the wholly basic requirements of the daily life of our people. Through the school boards which are associated with the municipal councils in the local activities, they must deal with problems of education as well as public works, public investment, streets, sewers, water supplies, light, unemployment relief, housing, health, welfare, their portion of the main provincial and county highways and many other services which are more intimately associated with the daily needs of each one of us than many of the very important things that we are called upon to deal with here.
3394	HOUSE OF
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities
The costs and responsibilities of local governments have soared beyond belief and they show every sign of increasing enormously within these next few years. The resources available for municipal governments are neither adequate nor flexible enough to produce the revenue which they need. As we think of this problem and as we consider the ways in which it does fall within the possible action of this parliament to do something about it, we should project our minds forward to what is going to happen in the years very soon ahead of us in order to contemplate what may happen unless something is done and done very soon. By 1975 or quite soon after that date there are reasonable prospects that this country will have a population of 30 million people. We see evidence of an increasing movement of population to the urban or suburban areas. We see the increased need for internal transport facilities within municipal areas that are expanding rapidly into the suburban areas as well as part of an integrated plan of development.
In addition, there are many new needs which will arise. Already it has been necessary for some of the provinces to consider the need for special supplies of water to meet the domestic requirements because of the enormous demands on the ordinary water supply which is not adequate to meet the greater size of the urban communities. It is simply beyond the ability of municipal governments to meet these responsibilities within the limits of their present revenue resources.
Some new methods must be found. There must be some adjustments to ease the burden. There must be some adjustments to facilitate their work. As the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) mentioned before, repeating what I had occasion to say not long ago elsewhere, we must remember at all times that there are the provinces and we must remember that the municipalities, to use the classic expression, are the legal creatures of the provinces. We must recognize that under our federal system the laws governing the provinces in relation to their municipal activities are provincial laws. Nevertheless there are ways in which things can be done by this parliament at the instance of the government of Canada which would assist them greatly at this time.
We have been told publicly as well as in presentations to the federal government that the government must take a more realistic view of the present situation and the new situation with which the municipalities will be confronted. The offers that have already been made for financial adjustment between the Canadian government and the governments of the provinces have been described
[Mr. Drew.)

as unrealistic. They have been described in other terms in different parts of Canada. One of the things that is certainly clear, and clear beyond all question, is that the present proposals which have been made in that field will not meet this urgent need of the municipalities.
One of the places where the parliament of Canada can do something effective is with regard to sales taxes and other excise taxes on purchases by municipal governments. There is something that is the direct and exclusive responsibility of this government and of parliament. Having regard to the fact that it involves a money problem, any move to solve this question must come from the government. They must be prepared to indicate their willingness to deal with it if it is to be dealt with at all.
Then there is another matter that comes entirely under the jurisdiction of this parliament and of the government. That is the situation created by the increasing area of land that is held by the government in the various municipalities and which is therefore exempt from taxation. There is a long history in regard to this situation which need not be repeated at this time. Naturally the municipalities welcome the services which are given by many of these crown corporations or other crown bodies. The fact remains, however, that as the land area taken over in this way increases, it does also accentuate the problem and the difficulties faced by the municipalities themselves. One of the things which most strongly emphasizes the unreasonable nature of this tax is the fact that where the very same things are bought by the provincial government they are exempt from taxation. I know there are certain exemptions. I know that there are exemptions under certain conditions in the case of road-making machinery and equipment of that kind. But generally and with very few exceptions the municipalities are taxed for all the equipment they buy which is needed for the people of Canada.
After all, nearly all the people of Canada live within the boundaries of some municipal body. Nearly all the people of Canada are greatly concerned at the present time with the rapid increase in the level of taxation. Nearly all Canadians are therefore directly affected by taxes on things which they need for their own daily use and which are not in any way part of ordinary daily trade or in any way luxuries or things that any of these people can do without. The municipalities require them for the actual needs of the people themselves.
I believe it is contrary to the whole principle underlying the imposition of sales

tax and of excise taxes that they should be imposed upon equipment, machinery and things of that kind or supplies of any kind bought by the municipalities for the use of the people themselves. Unless this were contrary to the underlying principle which guides governments in the imposition of taxes of this kind, there surely would have been no reason for exempting the provincial governments from the application of these provisions. The very fact that provincial governments were exempted emphasizes the acceptance by this government of the proposition that these taxes would not normally apply to things of this kind. Why should municipalities and the school boards within municipalities be called upon to pay sales tax and excise taxes on school equipment used exclusively for education as well as on equipment which is required for the service of these schools?
Certainly the government of Canada and the parliament of Canada must not invade the field of provincial jurisdiction where it is exclusively conferred upon any province under our basic constitution. This, however, is something very different. The government is constantly asked to help in education. Here is one way in which it can do so without any question of jurisdiction arising at all. By exempting school equipment, school supplies and the things that are needed for our schools there is given a direct and immediate assistance in the field of education and entirely within the realm of federal jurisdiction. When the provincial governments are exempted from these taxes, it seems strange that you should come to the boundary of the municipality and find that, just outside, exactly the same activity can be carried on with equipment or machinery that pays no tax of this nature whereas right inside the boundary the same machinery or equipment must pay this tax. All these people live within the provinces and they all live under provincial laws, whether they be laws applying to the activities of the province as a provincial body or to the activities of the municipalities as bodies set up in law by the provincial legislatures. Surely here is one case where we may well ask why this unfair tax is imposed.
There has been much discussion here about the cost of health. This government has been discussing ways in which it can assist in the field of health. Surely there can be no reason of any kind for medical supplies used by the health services in the municipalities being called upon to carry sales tax and excise taxes. It is imposing a senseless and onerous burden upon the municipalities in their carrying out of an essential and necessary responsibility.

Then let us examine the case of crown properties. These have been expanding constantly. With new types of construction, and with new development of the activities of the Canadian government, the area occupied by the Canadian government in many fields has expanded enormously. Whatever method may be devised, there should be adopted some method which will make available to all municipalities the equivalent of the local taxes on the property taken over in this way by the government of Canada on behalf of the people. It is no answer to say that these services are for the general welfare of Canadians. They are. But this is a type of tax that was intended for some entirely different purpose. This is a type of tax that was intended to apply to things that people themselves as individuals buy and sell. I can only repeat my argument that had that not been the case there would have been no reason whatever to have exempted the provincial governments from the application of these taxes.
It is quite true that if the government should give favourable consideration to this proposal-and I would strongly urge the favourable consideration of a proposal which has been put forward on a number of occasions and which I put forward very earnestly today-that action still would not meet the immense needs of the municipalities at this time. Nevertheless, it would be a positive start. It would be evidence of the intention of the government of Canada and the parliament of Canada to recognize within the field of its own jurisdiction the needs of the municipalities and what should be done.
This is not a subject which we raise here for the first time, Mr. Speaker. This is not a subject which we alone have raised from time to time. It is a subject that is being discussed in every part of Canada. It is particularly a subject that is being discussed by the municipalities right across Canada. This year there was presented to the government of Canada by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities a brief which sets forward the needs of the municipalities in a comprehensive, understandable, reasonable and very moderate manner. One of the points raised in this brief suggests another place where the government of Canada might give a lead in dealing with these problems. It asks that consideration be given to making operative again the Municipal Assistance Act of 1938.
I am not going to argue whether that act, in detail, should be made fully operative today.
I mention merely that the very responsible body which is described as the Canadian

Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities Federation of Mayors and Municipalities had this to say on page 9 of the brief:
Another resolution of the federation's 1955 conference calls upon the federal government to again make operative the provisions of the Municipal Assistance Act, 1938, in order that funds may be made more available to municipalities at low rates of interest for the construction of self-liquidating projects.
This act, Mr. Speaker, provided for finances from the government of Canada to municipalities for self-liquidating projects such as water works, sewage disposal systems and things of that kind. The act called for the co-operation of provincial governments, and under that act certain sums of money were advanced in different parts of Canada prior to the outbreak of the second world war. Under that act money was made available at 2 per cent interest for these self-liquidating projects. I am not going to argue today what the interest rate could be or should be in such an act.
I point out that here again is an example of the way in which the government of Canada can take steps to assist the municipalities within their constitutional jurisdiction in matters of this kind. Certainly it would greatly help municipalities at this time if funds were available at substantially reduced interest rates for public development.
In any event, whether or not that particular act be considered, the very fact that this recommendation is made by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities is in itself evidence of the urgent demand they are making for assistance and co-operation at this time. As I have said before, exemption from the sales tax and other excise taxes, payment of the equivalent of municipal taxation on crown property, and the introduction of legislation such as that to which I have referred, would not in itself solve this tremendous problem. It would, however, greatly help. It would end the plundering of the municipalities, and it is nothing less than that, under a tax which was meant for an entirely different purpose from that which is under consideration here. I think it is of immense importance at this time that we devote our attention in every way we can, within the limits of our fullest jurisdiction, to the needs of the municipalities.
I think it is also vitally important that in the arrangements that may be made with the provincial governments consideration should be given to the position of the municipalities and the need for opening wider areas of taxation for municipal councils than are now available to them. There is certainly nothing imaginary about this problem. It is being discussed right across Canada; it is being considered, and it is causing very

great concern. We have had reason, in these last few days, to think a great deal about the strength of our own free system of government. We have seen emphasized in different ways the distinction between our democratic system and a system which is entirely contrary to that under which we live. One of the things, it seems to me, that could well be borne in mind in considering this tremendously important subject is that the municipalities are, in fact, the places where democracy finds its greatest strength. The municipal body is, in fact, the cradle of democracy. Municipal government existed before national governments. Municipal government is closest to the people. Municipal government should be free in every way that is possible from any restraint upon the exercise of the judgment and good common sense of those who are elected to deal with municipal affairs in the various municipal councils. The strength of our democracy in Canada will be measured to a great extent by the extent to which we preserve the flexibility, independence and financial strength of these municipal organizations.
It was with that thought in mind, as well as the urgent and compelling needs that have been expressed by representatives of the municipalities, that I brought this subject before the house. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that immediate consideration should be given to measures to assist the municipalities of Canada to meet their mounting financial problems, and in particular the immediate introduction of legislation which will provide for the exemption of all municipal councils and school boards from the payment of excise taxes including the 10 per cent sales tax. and which will further provide for payment to municipalities of the equivalent of full municipal taxes."

There are many members of this house, Mr. Speaker, who have been members of municipal councils and I think, therefore, that many of us will have complete sympathy with the representations made by the mayors and municipalities to the Gordon commission and elsewhere, and indeed with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and the suggestions he has made for the relief of the municipalities. It is incongruous that the central government of Canada should tax the junior governments for supplies they need to carry on their activities in the municipal and provincial fields. The suggestion contained in the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition as outlined in the amendment to relieve them

of such imposts, is one which should command the attention of the Minister of Finance and the support of all hon. members; therefore, I am very glad indeed to support it.
The other proposal that the federal government should pay to the cities amounts equivalent to the tax-free buildings and properties in the various cities is also one which we can consider favourably. I would suggest, however, that in many instances the municipalities themselves should reconsider their own position regarding the tax-free properties in their own areas. Many of the municipalities, in order to entice business and sometimes to compete with other municipalities in the acquisition of new industries in their areas, have made very substantial exemptions. If the federal government is asked to review its position regarding tax-free properties now owned by the federal authority, the municipalities should be expected also to consider their own position regarding the tax-free properties in their areas. Not only have they tax-free property, but in some areas municipalities have given very favourable rates, renewable from time to time, in electric power, in water supply and in other respects. All these grants which they have made in order to obtain industries have complicated the question of municipal financing. The whole problem of tax exemption of industrial properties, of federal properties and of the concessions that have been made from time to time by the municipalities themselves should be very carefully reviewed. To the extent that the review relieves the local taxpayer in the municipalities of the heavy burden which he now carries, to that extent will the municipal finances be strengthened.
As a matter of fact, in recent years the municipalities have been called upon to carry tremendous burdens of expenditures. Thirty, forty or fifty years ago there was no heavy trucking, for example, and the cities did not need to maintain the kind of streets they now have to maintain, nor did the provinces have to maintain the kind of highway systems they now have to maintain in order to carry the heavy loads and so oh. Our cities have grown and so have the problems of water, the problems of sewage and the problems of health. When we think of the problems of sanitation-I am not going to say very much about that this afternoon- we think of the Ontario rivers and the way in which they are polluted. More particularly in my mind at the moment is the pollution of the great river which flows right beside where we are this afternoon in this parliament building, where the sewage from 230,000 people on this side and about 50,000 on the other side of the river empties in a raw state
30, 1956	3397
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities along this river all within four or five miles of this parliament building site. Many cities have tackled this problem; this city has not. Others have sewage disposal works. All of this has increased the burden of taxation. I suppose the capital city of Ottawa is waiting for this parliament to dispose of its sewage for it, but that is by the way. The suggestion is made that if the sewage gets very much stronger it might dispose of parliament. There is more truth than fiction in that because one of the embassies here has to keep its windows closed on hot summer afternoons now because of the stench arising from the river. It is an impossible situation and one which I hope that the city of Ottawa itself will be inclined to tackle.
But what I was going to say is this. When we think of the expenditures that the municipalities have to make for sanitation, for roads, and so on, not forgetting of course the tremendous expenditures that have to be made for education we begin to appreciate their problem. We realize that the provinces have increased their grants very substantially to the municipal councils in the field of education; but the provincial governments are strained to the very limit in that respect and the municipalities are finding it almost impossible to provide all the facilities that should be provided in modern communities and to meet adequately the costs of education.
When we think of the various federal, provincial and municipal authorities' expenditures, exclusive of defence and veterans' expenditures, which can be placed in a separate category, we find that the municipalities collected only 17 per cent of the taxes-and I am using the 1951 figure taken from Dr. LaZerte's report on educational costs in Canada. Included among their expenditures were 65 per cent of the local education costs; 88 per cent of the gross expenditures for public welfare, which came out of the municipal pot; and 72 per cent of the cost of roads, highways, bridges at the local level. When one thinks of that one can see how these necessary services to the people of the municipality and indeed to the people of the country inflict a tremendous burden upon the local taxpayers. Then, we have to remember also that most of these municipal taxes are collected on real property, with the result that taxes on real property, on homes and the lots on which the homes stand, have reached a very high level indeed; so much so that the taxes alone today are equivalent to what was a fair rent for a house say 30 or 40 years ago, when some hon. members like myself set up a home in this country.
Taxes on real property have increased by leaps and bounds. The limit of taxes on real
3398	HOUSE OF
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities property has not only been reached, it has been passed. The municipalities have nowhere to look for increased revenues. In some of the cities and in some of the provinces sales taxes have been introduced. The sales tax is a most unfair sort of tax even when it is earmarked for a specific purpose, we will say, for education or for health; but the provinces have been driven to it; they could find no alternative. In some of the provinces of course the sales tax now reaches 5 per cent or more on a long range of articles to supplement provincial and, as I have said, in some cities even municipal taxes. For example, in the city of Montreal there is a city sales tax, with the result that when you add it to the provincial sales tax you have a very high sales tax indeed. That sort of tax, of course, hits the family man very hard indeed because, with his larger family, he must buy more of the things the family will need in the way of clothing, and so on. Therefore, the discussion now before the house is one that is very worth while.
I would hope that within a measurable period more of the burden of health and of education would be assumed by this parliament. When I say education I know I am going to be immediately accused by some people of wanting to exercise federal control over our educational system. I see nothing incompatible with making grants for educational purposes to the provinces and through the provinces to the municipalities and provincial control of the curriculum, teachers' qualifications, complete control of education facilities, and the courses of studies and so on used in the schools in the various provinces.
As the days pass I think local authorities will expect us to assist in the field of health and education to a greater extent than before because after all health and education are not matters purely of local concern. I think the health of the nation is a national concern. A healthy population means that we have young men and women and people in middle life who are able to produce efficiently and continuously. Ill health not only means that we have to carry a heavy burden of hospitals and sanatoria but it also means that we have thousands of men and women who are out of production in what should be the prime of life and the economic loss to the country is very great indeed. The municipalities that are now bearing a considerable proportion of the cost of health services will properly, I think, seek relief through the provinces and the provinces will seek relief through the federal parliament of Canada in order to meet the heavy but vitally necessary burden of health services. The same is true


regarding education. Education is no longer a matter of local concern. I suppose that 40, 50 or 60 years ago a young lad going to school probably thought of settling down in his home community and spending the rest of his life there; very large numbers of them did just that. Today, however, it is different. Communications enable people to travel. Opportunities occur for the abilities of people outside of their old community and they tend to move in that direction. Education becomes not a matter of local concern but a matter of national concern.
We are told that we are faced with the competition of new nations that are promoting education and perhaps particularly scientific education. May I say immediately that I am not one of those who believe that scientific education should be the sole aim of our schools and universities. I think scientists should have a good grounding in the humanities if they are going to be good citizens and indeed if they are going to be successful scientists. When we think of the competition we are going to face in future years we realize that we have to provide more and better educational facilities. The municipalities and the provinces have a right to look to the central government of Canada for assistance in carrying this load and I hope that ere long the nations of the world will agree to measures of progressive disarmament.
When we have progressive disarmament and less expenditure in that particular field, I hope we shall be able to continue our level of revenue to the federal authority. I hope also that our increased output, our increased gross national product, the application of automation in our industries and the further increased output in that respect will mean that we may have larger revenues available to all levels of government. These will be largely available to the federal authority because of the manner in which the field of taxation is allotted in this country so that greater revenues will accrue to the parliament of Canada. Consequently ways and means should be found in which to assist both the provinces and municipalities in carrying the tremendous load which is imposed upon them because of the nature of our society at the present time and the nature of the activities in which our society is engaged.
Without taking more time I wish to say that as far as I am concerned I support the idea behind this amendment. I am not sure that it is as comprehensive as I would like to see it and I am not sure whether it is feasible in all respects. Articles that are

necessary for the municipalities, educational institutions and the provinces should be tax free. We should not have excise tax, sales tax or tariffs on goods that are going to be used by our public bodies and public institutions. As I said earlier, I think the municipalities as well as the federal authority and the provinces should consider the effect of the tax exemption policy that the municipalities and provinces have followed and the parliament of Canada has demanded.
We have tremendous tax exempt properties, some of which are railway properties. The Canadian Pacific Railway, for instance, is the beneficiary of tremendous tax exemptions in this country and they are in perpetuity. I do not say whether or not as time elapses the recognition of something given in perpetuity under entirely different financial and economic circumstances should be reviewed by the authority which first granted those exemptions. After all, a life sentence imposed upon a criminal does not always mean a life sentence; often it can mean less than 20 years with good behaviour. Perpetuity should also have some determination as the society in which it was granted under different circumstances develops and grows and the burden becomes a heavy one; therefore, I am supporting the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, in raising this question the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has done a service. We feel that it is a timely question, one which should be given every consideration by the hon. members of this house.
I believe, as was expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), that the amendment is perhaps not as comprehensive as it could have been but it is in terms which we can support and I rise at the moment to place our position on the question before hon. members in the hope that we might be able to obtain some sympathetic consideration of the problems of the municipalities and the provinces by this government at a time when it is giving careful consideration to the whole field of taxation and the division of taxation powers as between the federal government and the provinces.
I am not going to repeat the things which were said by the two previous speakers, but I do agree with them when they say that one of the great problems facing every province today is the deteriorating condition of the municipalities. Taxes levied against property by the municipalities have reached the point where they have become expropriatory, and I do not think I can describe them in any other way. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has said, we are
30, 1956	3399
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities away beyond the point where property in a country like Canada should be expected to pay. It simply means that in most municipalities taxes are so high that one must consider handing over to the municipal authorities the whole of his property every 20 years, and oftentimes more than that. That is a rather serious condition. Property cannot continue to bear the weight of taxation which it is now bearing in many provinces. Provincial governments have become increasingly aware of the seriousness of the situation and some of them are trying to do something about it. There are various things which the federal government could do to help this whole situation. I am not overlooking the fact that already something has been done, but in my judgment it does not go far enough to relieve the situation to the extent to which the federal government could do so.
May I outline about six or seven things which in my opinion could be done. When I mention these things I am fully aware of my responsibility in this house. Further I want it known that we are not simply talking about things when we mention these, for we have done something about this in my province. In my province we are trying to practise what we preach. As I go along I shall illustrate the things which I think the federal government can do by showing what we have done in my own province to relieve the terrible burden of taxation and debt which is now upon the municipalities.
First, it seems that many years ago the federal government put through legislation known as the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act under which municipalities were enabled to borrow under what were called successive guarantees granted by the provincial and federal governments at the rate of 2 per cent. Those loans were mainly for self-liquidating projects and were made for a period of several years. The act worked well and there are still some outstanding accounts, but I believe they are up to date. Every one is current and the government has not lost a penny through the operations of this act. I believe it has proved itself to be an effective piece of legislation in every way. I can recall my experience as provincial treasurer in the province of Alberta in dealing with loans under that act. I know the great good that we were able to do with the assistance of the act.
With the onset of world war II the act was suspended and no further loans were made. I submit that there is no reason in the world why that act could not be revived and operations under it continued. If there ever was a time when it was needed it is today. Municipalities are hard pressed to
3400	HOUSE OF
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities get money to carry on the vital services of the municipalities as well as money with which to finance the expansion of services occasioned by the large increase in population which many of them have experienced over the past few years. Consequently it would seem to be only logical that where they are forced into the field of borrowing we should do something about reviving the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act and grant the municipalities the right to borrow with provincial-federal assistance at a lower rate of interest.
I do not say that it would be possible to lend money to them at 2 per cent as we did prior to world war II, but certainly we should lend them money at a much lower rate of interest than they are having to pay when they go into the money markets of the world and compete against one another for the sale of their debentures. There is no sense or rhyme or reason in forcing municipalities to pay 51, 6 or 6J per cent on money that they must borrow. Normally they cannot sell their debentures at a figure less than 6 or 6J per cent. I would certainly urge the federal government to consider reviving that act.
There is another thing I would mention. Much has been said here about federal assistance in the building of roads. I did not speak when the trans-Canada highway bill was being considered, but I had in my mind some things that could have been said but were not said. One thing I should like to draw to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is that his department and other departments of the government are taking large sums of money in the form of taxes from the automobile industry of this country. If the figures which I have been able to gather for 1954 are correct, and I think they are, in that year the federal government collected $257 million from the automobile industry in the form of excise, sales and other taxes.
It then becomes a question of considering how much was spent in the building of roads. If the minister will go into the record he will find that less than $20 million was spent in the building of roads in Canada in that year. That seems to me to be a pitifully small percentage of the income derived from the automobile industry which wears out the roads. It seems to me that the responsibilities borne by the municipalities of this country are so great that the federal government could well afford to turn back in some way through the building of roads or a network of highways, or in the form of assistance to the provinces in the building of highways other than the trans-Canada, a larger proportion of


the income from the automobile industry. That seems to me to be the only logical thing to be done.
I think a tremendous weight of evidence has been presented here in the past week or two since I came back to my work to bolster up the contention that the responsibility of the federal government in this field of highway building is very great. I would suggest that here is one field that could be explored to good advantage. Perhaps the minister and his colleagues could get their heads together and find out how they could return to the municipalities a greater portion than the $20 million as compared with $257 million of the taxes taken out of the automobile industry. So much for that.
May I say just a word about the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition which asks for the removal of the sales and excise taxes applied against the things purchased by municipalities and school divisions. I can recall years gone by when members of all parties on this side of the house urged the government to do just that. We presented arguments which it seemed to me were logical in favour of the removal of these taxes. I stand today where I stood when I first mentioned this seven or eight years ago. I believe the time is long past due for the removal of these foolish taxes.
For example, take a school van operated by a school division for the purpose of carrying children to school. When a school division buys such a van they must pay a fairly substantial amount of money in the form of excise and sales taxes. When a municipality buys a bulldozer or a caterpillar tractor for the purpose of building roads-

They do not now? How long is it since that was removed? It must have escaped me.

That was one of the onerous items for a long time. Then we have building supplies. There is one example with respect to which there is, of course, no question that they do pay. These municipalities and school divisions are having to spend huge sums of money to provide buildings for the increasing population of the country. I see no logical rhyme or reason why these people should have to pay sales and excise taxes on building materials. It seems to me that a 10 per cent sales tax in the case of that sort of thing is like exacting from one of your children a 25 cent fee to enable him to come to the dinner table or the breakfast table. I think it is quite comparable, and

it seems to me the tax should be removed entirely so as to give these people a chance. At least that is one item that the federal government can consider with some sympathy, and if they would see fit to remove these taxes it would certainly be a great help to the municipalities. It would help them to avoid any further onerous taxation against property or the imposition of sales taxes.
There is one other thing I think the government can do. One could talk for the whole of one's allotted time in a debate like this on the decentralization of industry. Over the years we have watched a centralization of industrial activity in the larger cities. These industries pay taxes there and, of course, they create problems, including the problem of the fouling of water and all that sort of thing. But there are many municipalities where you find no industry at all.
If the government were to follow the advice of General Worthington, who is in charge of civil defence, it would take the lead and would assist the provincial governments in trying to work out some systematic pattern of industrial development so that there would not be this dangerous centralization. If that could be done it would help the municipalities of the provinces to a very remarkable degree. This government can take the lead. There are many ways in which it can take the lead. By wise direction from here I am certain that a movement towards the decentralization of industry could be worked out which would benefit the municipalities to a tremendous degree.
Let me say a word about education. I support what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said. In spite of the fact that there are those who feel that when anyone here mentions federal aid for education they are trying to interfere with provincial autonomy, I still think that there are ways by which the government can advance substantial aid to education that would assist the municipalities in no mean degree. I think the time is long past when that should be done.
I was taking a look a few minutes ago at the terrific cost of education in the provinces, and I want to say that when one contemplates not only what the school divisions in the provinces are having to pay today to educate children but also what they are going to have to pay in the next few years when the full force of the post-war population begins to have its impact upon the schools, believe me, they are going to face an almost overwhelming problem. It seems to me, without going into a dissertation on federal aid to education, that there is another field in which the federal government can help to relieve the terrible burden

Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities upon the provinces and municipalities, particularly the municipalities. They are the ones I am thinking of at the moment because they are the ones who have to carry the great burden of costs for education.
Taking a look at the seven fiscal years ending March 31, 1951, through to March 31, 1957, I notice that in my own province the provincial government over those seven years has made operational grants to the schools totalling $104,641,791, construction grants to schools totalling $22,871,929, and grants to the teachers' retirement fund amounting to $4,333,739. That is just in seven years. But that does not, of course, account for the full cost of education by any means. As I have already said, with the tremendous number of boys and girls who are now just about ready to enter our schools following the postwar upsurge in population, the municipalities and school divisions are going to have a pretty tough time.
What about our universities in future years?

Yes, in another ten or twelve years the universities are going to be in exactly the same position. In fact, they are feeling the impact right now. Certainly we should be forward looking and make provision ahead of time for these heavy burdens that will have to be carried.
May I say a word about another way in which the federal government can certainly be helpful to the municipalities. The other day my hon. friend, the usually forthright Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), was asked a question concerning the rediscount rate, and I was surprised that he did not give us more information than he did. I thought he evaded the question and I was sorry because, as I say, he is usually a pretty forthright fellow. There must be some reason behind the increase in the rediscount rate to 3 per cent. If there is not, bless my soul, why let it take place then? Surely this is the sovereign body and the Bank of Canada is not our sovereign master. At least, I do not look upon it as such and we ought to be laying down the policy for the Bank of Canada and not the Bank of Canada for this house and the country.
It is all very well to get the advice and counsel of the Bank of Canada. That is fine. But let me show you what they have done. By increasing the rediscount rate to 3 per cent they have put an almost impossible burden upon the municipalities and school districts that have to borrow. They are forcing these people to have to go out in the debenture market and sell their debentures at a great discount and at an effective interest rate that will run to 6, 6J or 7 per
3402	HOUSE OF
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities cent. If, Mr. Speaker, the government really wants to do something to help the municipalities it will take hold of that rediscount rate and see that it is not used as a means to bolster up the interest rates charged by the banks in this country for the simple reason that the municipalities cannot pay it.
The municipalities have to finance in some way. In order to help to relieve that situation in my own province, the provincial government decided we would have to get into the field of lending and so we set up just last year a new corporation which is called a municipal financial corporation. It is a co-operative composed of membership from the cities, towns, the rural municipalities and the government. They each buy shares. The corporation then manages pretty well the distribution of financial assistance to the municipalities in the province. Whenever any municipality requires to borrow, an application is made to the corporation. The corporation does the investigating, decides on the terms and that sort of thing, and eventually out of a reserve fund set up by the province loans are made to these municipalities and school divisions with government backing at no higher than 34 per cent.
We have successfully obviated the necessity of our municipalities going into the money markets of the world and selling debentures there during the past few years because of the fact that they could not possibly pay the rate of taxes they have been bearing and at the same time carry the interest rate that would be charged for such debentures in the money market. We have saved them many thousands of dollars by that means. So, Mr. Speaker, as I said to begin with, I am not just talking one way and watching my own people in the province of Alberta act in another way. We are practising what we preach. I suggest that the Minister of Finance take under very serious advisement the whole question of the bank discount rate and do something to make it possible for our municipalities to borrow their needs at a rate of interest that will certainly not be 6 or 6J per cent.
The final point is this. Quite a number of years ago we recognized that if we were to be of any help to our municipalities in the province, one of the things we would be obliged to do would be to agree to pay taxes in full on provincial property in the towns and cities of that province; and that is what we have been doing. We have been making a grant that was not only equal to but in excess of the full amount of taxes which those municipalities would have charged against the provincial property at the usual assessment rate. I think the minister could take that as a good example. When he contemplates all


of the things that have been said here today with respect to help to the municipalities, I think he would be well advised to resolve to bring in a change to his act under which he would pay full taxes to every municipality in this country where there is federal property established. By doing so, he would be doing something worth while.
He will probably say he is not as fabulously rich as you are.

Maybe not. But it seems to me that he has plenty. I do not think he is in rags and tatters, by any means.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that this amendment is timely. It would direct attention to the terrible condition in which many of our municipalities labour today. I certainly suggest that all the minister needs to do is to ride up and down some of the streets of Ottawa-

I will just repeat what I have said. I gave a short answer to a question which I thought was directed solely to that short answer on the occasion, being under the impression that I was not expected to state at any length whatever the present monetary policy, particularly having in mind that-as I have said already three times, I think, Mr. Speaker-as before parliament opened we knew there would be questions about this matter, we made suitable arrangements and gave suitable notice that we would discuss this matter in the banking and commerce committee. I regret that that discussion has not yet taken place but that situation has been brought about owing to the fact that I personally desired that some of the legislation which had been sent to that committee should come back here to be passed on to the Senate for further consideration before we went into a subject which did not require their consent at a later date. As a matter of fact, some of the legislation is already out of date and is not renewed unless the legislation we have before the committee and before the house is passed.
On the main point at issue in this amendment, there are of course a number of features that ought to be discussed. First I will touch on the suggestions that have been made by all three of the hon. members who have spoken previously, namely that we ought to bring the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act into use at the present time. The Municipal Improvements Assistance Act was passed in 1938 as an unemployment measure designed to stimulate employment in Canada. It was intended as a bonus, if you will, to municipalities in order that they might undertake self-liquidating projects at that time, but always having in mind unemployment. I do not think anyone in this debate will suggest that 1956 is a year in which we need bonus the putting of people to work in Canada.
We hope not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Up to the present time there are no signs that that is so. In any event, it would be quite impossible at the moment to find many municipal corporations which would use the act even in its present form. I make that statement for this reason. On both occasions when the provincial premiers were here last year and once again when they were here this year this question arose. On each occasion I told them that if they had any instances of municipal corporations not being able to borrow money for needed municipal purposes, I should be glad to investigate the reference they would make. To this date I have not been given the name
30, 1356	3403
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities of a single municipality in this country that has not been able to borrow money for its purposes. It may well be that there are some municipalities which are obliged to pay more interest than they think they should pay on money borrowed for local improvements. I have no doubt that all of us would like to borrow money at a lower rate than that which we think we are going to be obliged to pay when we set out to borrow. The higher the rate, the more likely it is that the municipal corporation will give serious consideration to priorities in the municipality with respect to expenditures of the taxpayer's money. I would not want to express any opinion about that matter, however, because I do not think it is our duty-nor is it a privilege of ours-to express opinions about municipal expenditures. I merely urge again that unless municipal corporations find it impossible to borrow money or find it possible only on extremely difficult terms, there is no point in reviving the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act at least until another occasion when we may desire to stimulate employment by having public works at all levels.
The hon. member for Peace River described in some detail the arrangements that are being made in the province of Alberta with regard to the municipalities. I share the view that I thought the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) expressed by interjection, although I am not sure that I heard him correctly, namely that perhaps the province of Alberta was better off than I am. If that is what it was, may I say that I am inclined to think maybe that is so.
I said I thought you would perhaps say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then I have done so.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: The hon. member is not disappointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The province of Alberta is now in a position to make with its municipalities almost any arrangements that it might desire to make. They have the money in the bank and may do so. But the problem that faces the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) here at the moment is this, and it is always the same one that is presented by all opposition members. It would be utterly impossible to raise, by the present tax rate, sufficient revenue to carry out the proposals that they bring forward in the house.
We will have something to say here about that matter later.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will come to that. It may well be that the whole suggestion here might

It would amount to more than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That may be so, if you include the sales tax. I have not the figures at hand. But let us suppose the figure is $30 million or $40 million. It may be said that there is a surplus this year of $115 million and therefore one could do this. But the fact of the matter is that at every session of parliament hon. members opposite present proposals which run into the hundreds of millions of dollars rather than the tens of millions and the Minister of Finance is always in the position of having to say that it is not possible to implement them without an increase in the tax rate. At the same time hon. members opposite deplore the high tax rate and leave the minister in a position where his general approach to this problem is, I think, that he would rather not spend the money and reduce the tax rate instead of spending the money and maintaining the rate at its present high level. There are some exceptions and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has drawn my attention to the fact he has always indicated, and he is quite correct, that he believes this parliament could make greater expenditures and find the money available through the good offices of the Minister of Finance.
The hon. member for Peace River spoke of the wise direction by this government in decentralizing, I take it, the functions of government. Coupled with that, I might point out that the Leader of the Opposition said that the municipal corporations were the cradle of democracy and existed long before national government. I think perhaps on second thought he would agree that it was just the reverse in Canada. We had national governments of one kind or another and municipal corporations grew up afterwards as a result of various statutory enactments. It is true that municipal corporations, in any matter whatever affecting municipal corporations, are entitled to make representations to us. They are entitled to make representations to us to remove the tax burden on them, as they have done in the brief of the mayors and reeves, and we should give consideration to that. However, in the direction of their affairs or in anything whatever connected with them, I think every provincial government of this country would expect this parliament to adopt a hands off attitude.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And hands out of their pockets, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The leader of the Social Credit party also spoke of a figure of $250 million
[Mr. Harris.)

received from the motor car trade of Canada by way of taxes. My recollection of the figure with respect to the special excise tax only would be something of the order of $80 million or $90 million. I am not sure what the balance is, unless it happens to be the corporation income tax.
The 10 per cent sales tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I might point out that we seem to be considering taxes by the source rather than the purpose. This government, if it did not need the money for its general purposes, would no doubt be doing away with a great many taxes about which it could be said, as my friend has said, you should use them for purposes connected with the base of the tax. We are not taxing motor cars in order to build highways; that was not the purpose of the tax in the first place. The purpose of the tax was to pay for the war effort and subsequently to pay for the additional cost of defence and such matters as have been imposed upon us.
The municipalities have to pay for roads, and they wear out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The municipal corporations have to pay for roads, and so do the provincial governments. I am not even going to suggest that they ought to spend the precise amount of money they collect from motor cars, by licence fees, the gasoline tax or anything like that-
The Liberal opposition in the province says they should.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That may be, and that is their business in the provincial field. I am not going to argue here whether or not the proceeds of the tax ought to be spent precisely on the subject matter from which one gets the tax. Indeed, if that were so we would have a lot fewer taxes than we have.
Now, the leader of the C.C.F. party made a statement with which I think we can all agree, namely that health and education are not solely of local concern. Stated in that manner it only means that all of us are desirous of having a higher standard of health and education throughout Canada. Nothing that I would say at any time would indicate dissent from that view. But once again, sir, and especially with respect to education, there is no point in repeating what has been said so many times by this government. It is not our view that we should

raise money in parliament here for the purpose of paying it out for education in the provinces or in the municipalities. We do spend money for the education of Indians, and we do make grants to higher learning. We have not taken the view that we should impose taxes to make grants in this field, with the exception of the two items I have mentioned and vocational training.
The real purpose, I take it, of the motion is covered by the complaint that municipal corporations are losing money by reason of the operations of this government in the various municipalities, in that the municipalities have to provide services, lose the assessment and do not get grants in lieu thereof. Now, there are two problems to be borne in mind here. Once again the general problem, sir, is that if we were to pay out a greater sum of money we should have to take in a greater sum of money through the tax rate. It is a matter of opinion whether all the municipal corporations or the individuals comprising those corporations would prefer to have a lower federal tax rate or whether they would prefer to have the grants. I believe that is a matter on which there would be perhaps 200 different opinions in the house.
Let me point out what is done in another field. So far as I have been able to determine there are only two provinces which make anything like the type of payment it has been suggested this afternoon we ought to make. If the provincial governments, in their relations with the municipalities, their own creatures, do not feel justified in paying the municipal corporations it seems to me that there are some arguments why such payments are either unnecessary or undesirable.
I would not suggest, however, that our own views here would be coloured particularly by what the provincial governments might do because they would have perhaps different reasons for doing that from what we could advance to parliament.
But may I point out that Ontario, while it does pay the general rate on its property, does not pay the school rate. The Ontario hydro does pay the general and school rates, but not on buildings for operational purposes. The provincial government does not make a payment on behalf of the educational institutions. In Manitoba the provincial utilities pay the equivalent of both taxes on land and buildings, and the province pays full taxes on land but not on buildings. In Saskatchewan the provincial government pays full taxes, including business tax, on all the properties of crown corporations except the Saskatchewan power corporation and the Saskatchewan government telephones. In

In British Columbia, the power commission pays 3 per cent of its gross revenue and the provincial liquor board pays what it believes its actual taxes might be. There is a provincial grant to the city of Victoria. In Quebec the provincial government pays the water rates and certain maintenance charges on certain crown properties.
In New Brunswick there is quite a complicated system of payments, but that is not to suggest that it is not fair in any way. They pay half the cost of snow plowing or a dollar a head, and they reimburse the municipalities by paying about two-thirds of the cost of renewing the main trunk highways through municipal corporations. They contribute to certain bridges, to the repair of main highways and they pay certain costs for local improvements in local improvement districts which I suppose have no municipal governments. Nova Scotia pays to the municipalities containing land under timber lease 5 per cent of their dues, and the liquor commission pays tax equivalents. In Prince Edward Island no payments are made in lieu of taxes. This would indicate that the payments by a senior body to a municipal corporation are not by any means regular or uniform except in so far as it would appear that the provincial governments do not make payments themselves on the general rate except, as I have said, in the case of Ontario.
It was suggested by the Leader of the Opposition, perhaps unintentionally, that municipal corporations are losing a great deal of income by reason of the crown agencies of this government. It might be that in some cases that is true, but most of them make their own arrangements with the municipal corporation in which the property is situated. For example, defence production, central mortgage and atomic energy pay full or very close to full taxes to the municipal corporations in which the property is situated. The Polymer corporation gives a grant of approximately full taxes. In every case these arrangements are negotiated with the different municipal corporations concerned. In the case of Canadian Arsenals, the board of grain commissioners and the national harbours board, they pay less than full taxes, probably in the neighbourhood of one-half. Therefore, the chief complaint, I am sure, is that this government pays taxes only in those municipal corporations where the Municipal Grants Act applies.
