May I point out, sir, that this history of payment by the federal government is now only six years old and that it was this government and this party which began paying to municipal corporations in 1950, and for a particular reason. That reason may not be valid at the moment. It is a matter of opinion which I know will be argued later on in this debate; but it was advanced as an argument at that time that because of the great concentration of federal property in certain municipalities it was unfair that they should bear a burden that ought to be borne by the general taxpayer of Canada. The formula of making a grant in lieu of taxes, where the assessment of the federal government in any municipality exceeded 4 per cent of the total, was devised. That was clearly understood for the reasons I have given, namely, that because of national purposes we had to place certain federal property in that municipality and that, for national purposes, the general taxpayer might be expected to contribute some of the cost rather than have the local municipal taxpayer pay the whole cost of the services and the assessment of that property.
You may recall, sir, last year we introduced an amendment to the act which reduced the 4 per cent to 2 per cent, during the course of which we would extend the payment of taxes from something like 50 municipalities to almost 150 municipalities in Canada in which we have federal property. We have had less than a year's experience with the act and I would suggest, sir, that on that basis we ought not to extend its provisions further at this time.
I doubt whether I have covered all the points that have been raised by hon. members opposite, but there is one point made by the Leader of the Opposition which requires an answer, namely, that it is not by any means surprising or unusual that a local purchase by a provincial government should not bear a tax when the same local purchase by a municipal corporation should. It has been a principle of our constitution for as long as I can remember that one does not tax the crown in the right of the province, but that principle never extended to a municipal corporation or indeed to any other form of corporation. The distinction is there and has been recognized since confederation.
Perhaps I should add one word further about the sales tax on purchases by municipal corporations to remind hon. members that we also require a good deal of experience in this field. We have been collecting taxes for some time, sir, and on the basis of the experience which we had up to that time my predecessor introduced an amendment to the act three years ago in which he provided that


there would be exemption for certain road machinery and the like over $1,000 in value. It must be evident that one of the reasons why we were able to make that amendment was that items of this kind were clearly defined and could be clearly recognized as such. But I do not think, sir, that we should extend exemptions to all purchases made by municipal corporations for the quite obvious reason, which may not commend itself to hon. members but does commend itself to a minister of finance, that exemptions generally are undesirable.
The best form of taxation is a tax which requires no exemptions, not because one receives more revenue that way, but because in fact with exemptions you always have the argument that the exemption is discriminatory against someone else in a like position _ who ought to have the exemption as well. The whole basis of taxation is to find one in which you are not subject to any of these arguments. Because you gave an exemption to A, logically you must give it to B, and if you go on in that way long enough you find there is no basis whatever for the tax in the first place and you have to start all over again.
I am not trying to magnify the difficulties of the Minister of Finance because I suggest, Mr. Speaker, our tax system is reasonably good and does not create too many difficulties.
However, sir, I would like to conclude by saying that, as I promised the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) and other hon. members a year ago when we were discussing the Municipal Grants Act and the amendments I brought forward at that time, this subject is under constant review and will be considered not only at the moment but throughout the coming year. However, it is not the intention of this government to introduce any amendments to the Municipal Grants Act at this session.
May I just make this final point? These motions to go into supply do give an opportunity to all hon. members to debate a good many subjects and do give and are intended to give the opposition an opportunity to present an argument in most cases against the shortcomings-that is the omissions rather than the commissions-of the government; but at the same time it should not be overlooked that these motions are in themselves a statement by the opposition that this government has failed and ought to be dismissed from office, because that would be the result of the motion carrying. For that reason I feel just as firmly as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) does that this government ought to remain in office and for that reason I am going to vote against the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, the issue that is before the house is, as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) has said, a very timely one. It has been the concern of many people from coast to coast in this dominion. It has been moved again today by the Leader of the Opposition, who has had a wide experience on different levels of government. He has had experience as an alderman and mayor and also in local council work and realizes the tremendous burden that is being carried by the municipalities of this dominion. The mayors, school boards, reeves, aldermen, controllers and councils have had a most difficult time, and their future looks very alarming to them from day to day.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Peace River, and I was not surprised but glad to hear that they intended to support the amendment. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, many of us in this house have had experience in other levels of government, provincial and dominion. As I recalled the years that I spent in municipal affairs I could not help but think of the vast changes that have taken place during those years.
I have also listened with keen interest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris). I noticed that he searched the provinces, the hydro commissions, the liquor commissions and every other level of authority he could think of to find an anaemic excuse for not accepting the motion; however, he finally concluded by saying the chief reason for not doing so was to keep this government in power. Before he said that I knew that neither he nor his colleagues want to lose power, though if they were not jolted occasionally they would ride along in their smug complacency and do nothing for anybody other than themselves. They are the world's greatest optimists; one can imagine that they do not care what happens so long as it does not happen to them.
The federation of mayors, reeves and councillors throughout the country have been pleading with every hon. member of this house for many years, and I am sure they have not missed government members. I will venture to say that the Minister of Finance's wastepaper basket is full of petitions from coast to coast pleading with him for some assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I keep them; I do not throw them away in the waste basket.

Well then, that old pigeonhole must be chock full of dust and petitions, because you certainly have not done anything about them.

Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities
This is a problem which is common to all. Mr. Speaker. The changing times have placed tremendous burdens on the municipalities, burdens that were not thought of 25 or 40 years ago, as hon. members have already pointed out. I can remember years ago when I was in the county council. It is because of these increased burdens that the municipalities are in their present plight.
Even farmers buy new automobiles occasionally. A farmer buys a similar licence to that purchased by a city dweller, but the man who lives on a provincial highway has to pull his car with his tractor through a foot and a half of mud down the side road to get it on to the highway. He has to keep his hogs until they are too fat and no longer select because he cannot get a truck in to get them out. At various times he cannot get his cattle to market. These are problems which exist in many places; the municipalities cannot keep pace with the times. This is a real problem in rural municipalities, and it involves not only the standard of living but many marketing dollars.
Despite all these things we are given excuses concerning what can and cannot be done. We hear the constitution referred to, and we are told that it is the responsibility of the provinces or the municipalities. It is not entirely a case of jurisdiction, and I think an over-all revision of our revenue system and a new look at responsibility in view of the rapid growth and expansion of this country are long overdue. The provinces and the dominion should sit down together with the municipalities and attempt to work out an over-all agreement.
We realize that the municipalities are the creatures of the provinces and the provinces are the creatures of the dominion. The Leader of the Opposition said the municipalities are the real cradle of democratic freedom, because a great many people have gone from the municipal level of government to other fields of government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I graduated after you did.

Yes, I was looking at you. I noticed you too, and I recall that you graduated from a neighbouring county. I am amazed that you have so little regard for the municipalities after having been a county councillor, because any one who has spent some years on a county council usually develops an affection for it, not only for the duties performed by councils but for the pleasant social occasions which form a part of their activities.
Never before have the municipalities faced greater responsibilities, and never before have they received a smaller portion of the
3408	HOUSE OF
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities national revenue with which to meet them than is the case today. The Minister of Finance says they were given a little bonus in 1938 because of unemployment, but he is optimistic now and says there is not going to be any unemployment, and apparently he thinks that is ample excuse for not giving the municipalities any help today. He said it would not amount to very much if the sales tax were taken off and they paid the tax they should pay on their federal property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I excluded the sales tax from that. I was thinking of municipal councils.

In fairness to the minister I could agree with him, but this government has always said, "What is a million?" and now it says, "What is 20 million?" The government sits quietly by and does not even attempt to offer the relief that could be given under our present jurisdiction. The minister has pointed out that the liquor commissions and the hydro commissions pay the municipalities only a certain amount, but in most cases his government pays them nothing. It levies a sales tax on much of the equipment they buy and they are even taxed on municipal printing. The government takes all the tax it can from the municipalities and gives as little back as possible.
The government does not seem to take into account the growth and expansion of this country. With respect to all this national expansion and industrial development we must keep in mind that it is this forgotten level of government, the municipal level, which has such tremendous responsibilities at the present time. The development of industrial expansion, the building of industries in different places, the standards of services in the municipalities, all have a great bearing on the attraction of foreign capital and the location of industries in the respective districts. More and more the municipalities are becoming the cradle of our whole national industrial development.
As has already been pointed out, the municipalities must provide services for housing developments, educational institutions, must provide roads and so forth. Many other matters enter into this field including traffic congestion, the safety of children and so on. When you drive along the highway in this country you can always tell when you are at the edge of a municipality because you are likely to break a spring on your old Ford car or blow out a tire in the municipal pot holes. The municipalities are more or less curtailed in their ability to collect revenues.
I can well recall that when I belonged to the government that was in power many of the hon. members who are absentees today used to chide us for not being fair to the


municipalities. They said the municipalities were having a hard time. I can recall that the circumstances were difficult in those days because there was a world-wide depression, but at that time the government of Canada took only 40-5 per cent of the total revenue of the dominion. In 1951, 20 years later, the dominion's take had increased from 40 [DOT] 5 per cent to almost 71 per cent. At that time the provinces took 20-2 per cent, today they take only 17-2 per cent. In 1930 the municipalities had 39-3 of the total tax revenue, today they have only 11-9 per cent. Never has their responsibility been so great and never has their portion of the total revenue been so small. Yet this government sits smugly by and quietly and complacently takes a greater share of the revenue while at the same time enlarging its share of power.
We had a conference, a dominion-provincial conference. All these have been very nice parties. Everybody talks about a new approach and then they call a conference. It takes them a long time to decide to call it and it takes them a long time to assemble. Not long ago the federation of mayors were greatly encouraged when they were told that while they would not have much authority at the conference, they could come to it. They attended with a watching brief and were greatly encouraged as they thought something was going to happen, that the provinces and the dominion would make over-all federal-provincial agreements by which some relief would be given to the struggling municipalities, and a broad national policy might be inaugurated to provide some uniform assistance to them.
The federation of mayors may have had only a watching brief, but they certainly looked and listened and watched. They watched the slow assembly and they heard the quick adjournment. Nobody made anything or got anything. Nobody gave anything away. They were told quietly to go back home. Seldom in history had so many come so far for so little. There was no real effort, no new agreement; it was a mere mockery. No wonder municipal officers in places like Toronto were disappointed. They had wanted to have a conference a few months ago, and asked the Prime Minister to hold such a conference, but the answer they got was that even the Minister of Finance was too busy. Later on the Minister of Finance did send for them and brought them down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On the contrary, I went to see them.

For all the good it did, it did not make any difference whether you went to them or they came here. That illustrates the whole attitude of the government. It

is not the letter of the constitution, it is the spirit of the government. This tired old government is just the same on everything; it is just smug and complacent about everything. They are the greatest optimists in the world. They think it does not matter what happens as long as it does not happen to them. It is not a matter of this resolution, it is simply a matter of this government being so complacent. They fail to grasp the problems that confront us.
I do not mean to say that anyone who has any knowledge of all levels of government would say that the constitution could not be considered at all. We know there are the provinces and we know there are the municipalities. This present government seem to be interested in the provinces and apparently that is the reason only about half the government are here today. It must be because they are interested in provincial as well as dominion affairs.
I think there are ways under their present constitution that something could be done. As I say, the letter killeth but the spirit giveth. There are ways under their present jurisdiction that would permit them to do a great deal. This government taxes even municipal printing. They have been asked to relieve the municipalities of that tax. This government imposes the sales tax. They have been asked to relieve the municipalities of that tax. This government does not pay taxes on most of its properties. They have been asked to do so. The sales tax paid by some municipalities amounts to as much as $800,000. That may not seem much to the government here but it is something to the municipality, especially when the government pays nothing on its principal government buildings.
There are certain inequities in the grants that have been given in lieu of taxes under the Municipal Grants Act, which has been amended. I believe that about 100 municipalities receive a total of about $6 million.
I notice the minister is strong about no exemptions, fair play and equal rights for all, special privileges to none and so forth, but if he wants to put those principles into practice may I suggest that there are about 750 other municipalities which would get about $12 million if he treated them as he treats the other 100.
Then there is the unemployment problem, which has been mentioned before. This is not a tremendous problem at the present time, but for the man who has exhausted his coupons or who cannot qualify for relief unemployment presents a real problem. I suggest that unemployment should be considered as a national responsibility, and the dominion government should pay 100 per cent

This government is taking almost double the percentage of total taxes paid in Canada that was taken when this party was in power in 1930, while the municipalities take only
11-9 per cent today as compared with 39-3 per cent at that time. In other words in 1930 the provinces got almost 40 per cent of the total tax revenue in order to provide these services, while today this government takes over 70 per cent-
Nearly 80 per cent.

No, it is nearly 71 per cent, 70-9 per cent to be exact. They have gone from almost 40 per cent up to 70 per cent, almost double, whereas the municipalities are taking less than one-third of what they took of the take at that time. Who must bear the brunt of this? It is the home owner, the man who has a mortgaged house in the municipality. It is the head of the household who is trying to get his house paid for in order to have a home for his family. It is the working man. Those are the people who are doing it.
There is a limit to the amount of taxes that can be paid. A tremendous portion of our national production is being paid in taxation. I know it is argued by many economists, and sometimes just as vigorously by politicians who think they are economists, that still more can be taken because everything is sound. However, the problem of the municipalities is a growing one, it is a real one, it is a difficult one, it is one which must be solved for the health and prosperity of this dominion. The municipality may not be the cradle of democracy in the sense of being the cradle of parliamentary practice, but it is the cradle of industrial development. It is the cradle of the homes of this country, and the happiness and the family life of this country depend on the standard of living, to which reference has been made this afternoon.
Many more services are required. Streets in many municipalities are unsafe. You see children on their bicycles bumping over the holes in municipal streets and automobiles going by within inches of them. You see automobile tires blown out because of the condition of municipal streets. As has been mentioned this afternoon, right in this capital city we can see the evidence within ari eighth of a mile of this building. I notice that the way is fairly smooth from here to the Chateau Laurier, so that none of the government will be hurt. I am glad of that, because I walk that way quite a bit myself. But you

Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities do not need to go much farther down Rideau street before you find that you might as well walk as drive an automobile.
These are problems that concern the lives, the happiness and the homes of the people of Canada, and the municipal officers are confronted with these burdens. They are only receiving about one-third of the share of the national revenue they received 20 years ago, yet they are asked to provide many more services. This afternoon the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar emphasized the growing numbers of school children and what is required for educational services in the public and technical schools, indeed every branch of education from the kindergarten right through the university. We find that in rural municipalities the farmers are taxed almost double for the building of high schools and colleges that are being enlarged almost every year. Small municipalities within a few hundred miles of this city with a population of around 3,000 have spent as high as $1 million on educational services.
We are approaching 1958, 1959 and 1960 when, with the present rate of immigration and taking into account the birth rate and the increasing population, the requirement for educational services will be still greater. There is not one hon. member in the house who has not talked to municipal officers and been told about the ever-growing problem and the services that are going to be required. In view of the fact that the government's own revenues, their own taxes, depend to no small extent on the services provided by the municipalities and the condition of the municipalities, the government should reconsider its policy.
There is the question of the municipalities being able to attract new industries, and in that regard we should examine what the municipalities in the United States have done. We need policies in Canada to encourage the development of our resources and to enable our municipalities to attract industries. When these people from the United States come here to look at a municipality they are not encouraged to build in it if they see that it is short of schoolrooms for children, if they have to bump up and down the main street and pretty nearly break their Cadillac cars in which they drive over here to carry on their inspection. The revenue received by the Minister of Finance is affected accordingly.
Therefore I urge the government, and especially the Prime Minister, whether or not his luck has been bad, to try to get back to the days when his party talked about the great happy family of provinces. I remember


the billboards in years gone by:	"Vote
Liberal, one happy family, nine happy provinces."
That is still so.
They are pretty unhappy children now in many respects. The hon. member says they are still as happy.
You cannot see it.

I have heard some speeches in his province that did not indicate they were very happy. However, I urge the government in all sincerity, even if they have had a conference that has not accomplished anything, to sit down again with the provinces and discuss the matter. There may still be hope. If you cannot change the letter of the constitution you can change the spirit of your attitude and see the problem that is almost screaming at you so far as the municipalities are concerned. The municipalities are in distress. They are in a state where their progress is going to be hampered. The municipalities are asked to do more with less.
I have pleasure, Mr. Speaker, in seconding the amendment and supporting it. I am glad we have had the support of those to my left. I am sorry that so many to your right, Mr. Speaker, who would like to vote for this measure to help the municipalities are going to be forced to vote to save a tired old government from retirement.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the last words of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), namely that we are forced to vote for the government.
You know you are.
If that is the type of speech he is going to make, then I can tell him that he is far from being right.
Sure you are. Toe the party line.	'

I want to get down to earth, and I have two questions that I would ask the Minister of Finance to answer. Before I put them, may I say that I listened very attentively to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe and his description of the time when the party in power took 40 per cent of the nation's revenues, compared with the 70 per cent that we now take. Boy, Mr. Speaker, those were the golden days! Those were the prosperous days, were they not? I can tell you that I happen to know that, so far as our cities and municipalities are concerned, they do not compare with today.
At that time I could go to our schools, see how the children there were dressed and tell the brand of flour that was used in their

homes. We have better times today in our cities and all over Canada than we had in 1930 or later. I have two questions to ask the minister. If this amendment passes, you will have less money to spend, will you not? Therefore I ask the ministers, where are you going to get the money to replace the money you lose? What other taxes are you going to levy? If you do not levy new taxes, where are you going to cut down? I can tell you that you dare not cut down on veterans' pensions. Will you cut down on family allowances? Will you cut down on old age pensions? Will you cut down on unemployment insurance? Where are you going to cut? That is the question that bothers me.
I know that the mill rate has something to do with the taxes we pay in Fort William, but a whole lot of the success of the cities in which we live depends upon the city council. We have a city council in Fort William that watches finances closely. They watch spending. I do not know whether that is because there are three ladies on the council, but we have a council that watches spending closely. The amount of taxes I pay in Fort William depends on the mill rate, and if the mill rate goes up I pay more.
As far as the amendment is concerned, I just want to have these questions answered. Where are you going to levy any new taxes? Where are you going to make cuts? I do not want to see family allowances or old age pensions reduced, and certainly you cannot cut the veterans. As far as our veterans are concerned, there are some increases they should get and we are going to fight for them to the limit.
That is all I have to say. As far as my vote is concerned, nobody has told me how I am going to vote and nobody ever did. Perhaps they did that in former days, but they do not do it today.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to be brief and explicit in what I have to say. I think the amendment is very important, and deals with a very important question. I do not think it has anything to do with cutting any of our social service expenditures and I do not think it has much to do with dominion-provincial relations. I think it is a straight matter of proving to ourselves or some of the people to whom it still has to be proven that under the present scheme of things municipalities across the country are not able to carry the responsibilities fixed on them by the constitution.
In my judgment, if the amendment that has been proposed passes it will give very little relief to the majority of municipalities
30, 1956
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities throughout Canada. For a start, the resolution asks for the elimination of the excise tax and the sales tax on equipment and so forth purchased by municipalities. Most of the heavy equipment purchased by municipalities is now tax exempt. With regard to the other materials which they purchase, if the figures were worked out I do not think it would be found that the suggestion would give the majority of municipalities much tax relief. At the conclusion of the resolution we find these words:
. . . and which will further provide for payment to municipalities of the equivalent of full municipal taxes.
I assume what is meant by that wording is that in any municipality where the federal government has property, the full tax rate shall be paid. The wording is also subject to many other interpretations, but I think that is what is meant. If so, I want to say that 89 per cent of the municipalities across Canada would not receive any relief whatsoever, although some relief would be received by the larger centres where there is a concentration of federal property. I do not think the resolution offers much, Mr. Speaker. Before I sit down I intend to tell you what I think should be done instead of adopting the suggestions contained in the resolution.
I think we all must agree that the burden which cripples the average municipality across this country is the cost of education. That is the main problem. I know it exists in my own community to a great extent. For the first time in the history of the country, about three years ago we had a teachers' strike that spread fairly well over that whole community. Things are getting rather bad when people like teachers, with the qualities they have, find it necessary to strike in order to bring to the people who should know the situation a realization of the inadequacy of salaries. Right at the present time in that same area the teachers are demanding a commission to sit down with a school board in one municipality and try to work out more adequate salaries.
Being on the outside and not on the inside doing the fighting, one can see both sides of the argument. I recognize the problem faced by the municipality of which I am speaking in connection with meeting the demand for more adequate salaries. In that particular community a total of about 60 cents of every dollar collected in taxes goes into the schools, with the resultant crippling of other services. However, the municipality tries to carry that educational burden. Having 60 per cent of their total revenue going into schools is a terrific problem. Right at the present time they are in an extremely bad spot. Education

Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities is the crux of the problem as far as the municipalities are concerned and tax relief as suggested in the resolution will not help a great deal, except in the larger centres where there is a concentration of federal government property. The answer to the question of relief for the municipality in the field of education is federal aid to education.
I do not think it is necessary to sell that idea to any of the members of this house, regardless of the side on which they sit. However, the idea must be sold to the provinces. There are in Canada provinces which jealously guard their right to have complete supervision in the field of education. Unless you can get unanimity in the provinces I realize that the federal government is in an awkward position with respect to granting relief. If we do not give relief in the field of education, in my judgment any other gesture we may make will be only a palliative and will certainly not touch the crux of the problem.
Another way in which the federal government could help would be by accepting full responsibility for the employable unemployed. The 89 per cent of the municipalities that will not benefit under the formula proposed in the resolution are not in a position to carry the employable unemployed. I know that most of us who represent ridings away from Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and the larger centres find that when we are at home most of our time is occupied in trying to find employment for people who are unemployed and whose insurance has run out. There is no employment in the community and you spend day after day talking to them and listening to the sad stories; and they are sad ones.
There is nothing the town can do. The municipality has not the necessary finances and, as I said before, it is already staggering under the burden of trying to pay the bills for education. By accepting full responsibility for the employable unemployed the federal government would be making a gesture to the parts of the country in which revenues are the smallest; I refer to the municipalities. Of course in 1945 that offer was made by the federal government at a dominion-provincial conference that did not finalize any of the suggestions or offers made in the green book proposals at that time. The federal government, without changing the constitution, can help in that field of the employable unemployed.
The municipalities also have another burden, and it has to do with the field of health. That burden arises in connection with the indigent people of the community who cannot afford hospitalization or medical attention of
[Mr. Gillis.J

any kind. Most of the municipalities I have in mind have their own social service set-up in which people are paid to investigate and write little orders, which run into a great deal of money, without having complete responsibility for the indigent poor. They run into large hospital bills. Many of these people must be sent to other parts of the province. Then there is the matter of transportation, ward costs, nursing services and doctor bills. All that runs into a staggering figure in a municipality that has a population of 40,000,
50,000	or 60,000.
I have reference to the maintenance of the social service centre, the hospital ward costs, doctor bills and transportation for the indigent poor of the community. These are spots where neither the provincial government nor the federal government give any help. It is considered to be the burden of the municipality. The great majority of them, at least 89 per cent, are not in a position to meet those bills. That, of course, is something that should be taken care of through the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Most of the provinces are in this position; at least it is the position of the one in the end of the country from which I come. There is money available in the Department of National Health and Welfare provided they can match the grants, but it is the matter of matching the grants that deprives them of the opportunity of getting anything from the federal government. They have not the money with which to match the grants. I believe some formula should be worked out by the Department of National Health and Welfare with provincial governments to at least help in that field of providing social services and taking care of the indigent poor. That is another way in which the federal government could help by making use of the machinery that is already set up; and it would be some considerable help.
In that field of education also you run into the whole question of vocational training. That is something that is badly needed today. The press indicates a shortage of engineers, technicians and trained workers, that there is great need for them and all that kind of thing. There are in existence between the federal government and the provinces agreements that are very good, and a good job is being done where they can be applied. But in the end of the country about which I am thinking the difficulty is this. In order to get a vocational school started, a great deal of work and money is necessary. The federal government will pay 50 per cent of the capital cost of starting a vocational high school, but the province and the municipality between them must raise the other 50 per cent.

There are many municipalities that would have a vocational high school doing that kind of academic and vocational training if they were in a position to make their contribution; but many of them are not able to do so. I know centres in which they have studied the problem over the last 15 years and in which they have been willing and anxious to have these vocational schools. What has stopped them from getting them? The province is willing, the federal government is willing, but the municipality has not the money to pay their share of either the capital cost or the maintenance after the school is set up. They admit that quite frankly. I think, in time, the minister's department should sit down and take a square look at the equality of opportunity that exists in the field of education across this country, including these vocational training schools.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has already indicated that we intend to vote for this resolution. Personally I go along with him, and I will vote for it. However, I do not think it means very much. I am convinced that if the resolution were adopted it would mean very little to 80 per cent of the municipalities across the country, because in asking for tax relief mention is made of the sales tax and taxes of that kind. These things have been taken care of fairly well. We threshed that out for a number of years. The heavy equipment, like fire engines and bulldozers, purchased by municipalities is exempt from sales tax.
As I said before, wherever there is a concentration of federal property the municipality benefits considerably. Such municipalities are not the ones who need to benefit. The communities that need to benefit are those that are staggering under the load of education costs. Then there is the question of matching grants that are available providing the community has some money. The terms of this resolution would mean very little to those municipalities. However, in consideration of the little it does mean, I will go along and vote for it.
I would suggest the three things I have mentioned; federal aid to education; the federal government taking responsibility for the employable unemployed; and a square look at the whole field of matching grants by the Department of National Health and Welfare to see if something cannot be worked out under the present system to assist municipalities with their heavy load in connection with indigent people and social services.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
I, too, shall be brief this afternoon.
I do feel that the amendment which the Leader of the Opposition has put forward
30, 1956	3413
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities today is the best of the four which have been advanced so far this session by the Conservative party. I think this particular amendment is timely. I think it is fair and I think it is reasonable. Perhaps, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South suggests, it has not gone as far as some might like, but it is a motion which I think would be of tangible assistance to the municipalities.
In recent years, as every hon. member knows, most Canadian cities and towns have had ever greater difficulty in balancing their budgets. Since the war municipal taxes have been increased year after year. They have become so high in many localities that they are almost unbearable, yet the costs of municipal government continue to outstrip the revenues which municipalities are able to collect.
I must say that this afternoon I was not very satisfied with the reply the Minister of Finance made to the Leader of the Opposition and other members who have spoken. 1 feel that, in very polite language, he has given the municipalities the brush-off for another year. As I say, his language was courteous but it was a very firm brush-off nevertheless. I say the minister is once again refusing to recognize this very real problem, at least to the extent of giving tangible assistance.
I think this is to be regretted, because part of the difficulties under which municipalities are labouring has been caused by the fact that the federal government is taking such a huge proportion of the over-all tax dollar. Most of the new taxes which have been imposed since the war by municipalities have been on real property. As a result, in many areas of Canada today the burden is becoming so intolerable that the wisdom of even owning a house is becoming questionable. There are many people who say, in effect, "Taxes are so high we might as well rent."
A number of factors have been responsible for high municipal taxes since the war. There has been the inflationary period which has made the purchasing power of the municipal dollar dwindle. There has been the huge increase in population in our cities and towns, which has meant new streets, sewers, sidewalks, traffic lights, hospitals and so on. Moreover the increased population has meant that every city has needed more policemen, firemen, garbage collectors and so on. Most civic employees have demanded, and rightly so, fairly substantial wage increases in the past 10 years.
As has been already pointed out, the municipalities have been expected more and more to absorb certain welfare expenditures, such as costs for the employable unemployed, the costs of taking care of the aged, the costs of
3414	HOUSE OF
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities taking care of neglected children. All these costs have been increasing. Hon. members will have noted that since 1945 municipalities have frequently been called upon, in co-operation with the provinces and the federal government, to pay part of the cost of providing low-cost housing. It seems to me that these really are not expenditures for which municipalities should be responsible. Surely the senior governments should bear the full costs of these items. In any event these factors have stretched the credit of many municipalities in Canada to the very limit. In many localities they have pushed real estate taxes beyond reasonable limits.
What can be done? We have heard a good many suggestions this afternoon. Personally I think it is reasonable to ask the federal government to take the initiative in calling a dominion-provincial conference to discuss this whole financial problem of the municipalities. We could then see what could be done. I am absolutely convinced today that sooner or later the senior governments must explore the possibility of giving the municipalities a wider tax base.
In the second place, I think such a conference could consider relieving the municipalities of certain obligations which they have now, which are not particularly related to property ownership. Why for instance should the municipalities today be paying the costs of relief for the employable unemployed? Nor can I see why they should be forced to look after sick people, the aged and the like. As I said a moment ago, I feel these are responsibilities of the senior governments. Can anyone tell me why municipalities should have to look after civil defence? Surely that is an item which would fall within the jurisdiction of the federal government.
In the third place, and this has been mentioned already, I feel very strongly that the federal government should pay a normal taxation on all federal property in municipalities. The government has gone a long way in recognizing such a principle in the last few years, but many of the provinces still shirk their responsibilities. I think the provincial governments, as well as the federal government, should pay fair taxes on all their properties in municipalities.
The point has been made this afternoon that the government should exempt the municipalities from the payment of the 10 per cent sales tax on purchases they make. I certainly sympathize with such a proposition. It does seem ridiculous, as has been emphasized, that school boards and municipalities should have to pay a 10 per cent federal sales tax.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in this debate because this amendment deals not merely with $10 million, $20 million or $30 million but goes beyond that and suggests that consideration should be given to measures to assist the municipalities of Canada to meet their mounting financial problems. That to me is the real question and, like the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I feel it is a question which the minister has brushed off.
I noted some of the answers the minister gave, particularly to the hon. member for Peace River. In answer to something the hon. member for Peace River had said the minister expressed his view that the municipalities could still borrow. Well, I am not arguing against that, but to me that is not an answer to the question at all. To me it is not enough to say that the municipalities can borrow. What I am interested in is that

the municipalities should be put in a position to pay their own way. Borrowing just seems to me to be a palliative; it is just putting it off.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was discussing that part of his speech with reference to the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act.

I realize that, but I still think my comment is fair.
Second, the minister said-and I would agree with him-that there would be a great deal of questioning raised if the federal government stepped in to give directions to municipalities. I would agree with that, but that does not seem to me to enter into the matter at all. I agree that the municipalities are the creatures of the provinces, but I still feel the government is faced with a problem which is not met entirely by just holding back and taking a negative attitude.
My third point is that the minister answered the suggestion that the federal government should pay their taxes by pointing out that in some of the provinces that was not done; in some others it was only partially done. I have no doubt he was right, but I find that very unsatisfactory for two reasons. First of all, those other legislative bodies have limits as to their taxing powers. Second, I do not think this small and to me rather niggling excuse dealt with the main problem.
It is a long time, Mr. Speaker, since W. S. Gilbert wrote this little verse; it is close to 75 years ago:
Every boy and every gal,
That's born into this world alive,
Is either a little Liberal,
Or else a little Conservative.
I suppose some of us feel the political world would be a simpler place if that were still true; but it still is true that every boy and every gal born into Canada alive has the privilege of three forms of government to live under. Nominally, of course, all these forms of government are his servants. They are supposed to serve him, the taxpayer. Nevertheless it is a fact that they do not' always get on too well together. They do spend a good deal of the taxpayer's money in legal battles with each other, though not as much as previously. It would be interesting if we could find out just how much of the taxpayer's money has been spent by the various forms of government which he has set up in carrying out contests with each other. There was a period in the 1870's and the 1880's when one of the great industries of Canada apparently was litigation between the provinces, particularly Ontario and the dominion. Sir Oliver Mowat and Sir John A. Macdonald carried on continual controversy in those days, and of course we all remember occasions when
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities there was not always the fullest co-operation between the dominion and the provinces. We all remember that in the year 1930 the late prime minister of this country, in his famous five-cent speech, said, as reported at page 1227 of Hansard of 1930:
With respect to giving moneys out of the federal treasury to any Tory government in this country for these alleged unemployment purposes, with these governments situated as they are today, with policies diametrically opposed to those of this government, I would not give them a five-cent piece.
Those were some of the difficulties that we had, and it seems to me that we are dealing with this situation in what I find is a very disappointing way. We are not really looking at the matter with a broad enough view.
Let us agree that the municipalities are the children of the provinces. Sometimes they may feel like stepchildren; nevertheless the provinces have had to do and have done a great deal to recognize their needs and to support them. I find it difficult to describe actually the attitude of the federal government toward the municipalities. Perhaps one might say that they look on them as poor relations. My colleague the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) quoted from Charles Lamb a while ago to describe poor relations. I shall read one or two extracts from his remarks, as quoted at page 2871 of Hansard:
A poor relation is ... a drawback upon success-a stain in your blood-a blot on your escutcheon-a death's head at your banquet.
I do suggest very seriously that there should be and needs to be an entirely different approach to this matter. As I see it, plenty of evidence has been given in this debate this afternoon to show that the municipalities are really in a kind of impasse; and to say that it is to be left entirely to the provinces I find very unrealistic. The Prime Minister in his opening speech of the session said, and I quote from page 49 of Hansard:
In general, we did not see any need to share In the normal costs of growth of provinces and municipalities.
The word "normal", of course, is a word that could be debated a good deal; nevertheless I find that a very disappointing statement. I continue to quote from the Prime Minister:
The financing of this growth presented problems, but they did not seem to us to require a federal solution.
I shall try to argue later on that they do very much require a solution where all three forms of government come in, because if we have reached, as I suggest we have reached, an impasse so far as the municipalities are concerned, then what other course is
3416	HOUSE OF
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities there? Surely we are not going to regard the present situation of the municipalities as a normal feature of growth. Surely it is abnormal. Surely we do not believe we are in a constitutional straitjacket; surely we do not believe that it is impossible, if the need arises, to make some change whereby the municipalities will be able to live.
I suggest again that the attitude taken by the Minister of Finance this afternoon, following what the Prime Minister had said earlier in the session, is practically saying, "Now, there is a problem here but we are not going to have any part of it". I do not believe that can be the final word. I just cannot believe it and that is the reason I want to make whatever contribution I can to this discussion.
Here we have a taxpayer who is paying taxes to the municipality and to the federal government, leaving the province out for the moment. As the Leader of the Opposition outlined earlier, the taxpayer receives from the municipality a great many things including streets, education, sanitation, street lighting and police protection. I could go on and add to that. The federal government pays huge sums for defence, in which the taxpayer is concerned. It also provides family allowances when his children are young and an old age pension when he is old. Through the Minister of National Health and Welfare it provides circulars telling him what to take when he goes on a picnic and how to deal with baby talk and other things contained in various publications.
If the taxpayer is going to be put in the position where he finds that notwithstanding that he has to pay so much money to his federal tax collector there is not going to be enough coming to his municipality which is so close to him to enable it to do the things which are necessary, then he will very properly think we have reached a constitutional impasse.
I do not intend to dwell on the figures which have been given as to the extraordinary change which has come about in the last few years, but I shall just mention those figures briefly. In 1930 the municipalities collected $306 million and the provinces collected $157 million. It is difficult for us to realize that the provinces collected so much less then. The federal government collected $315 million in 1930; provincial governments, $157 million and the municipalities, $306 million. In 1951 the figures were: federal $3,791 million; provinces, $918 million; municipal, $636 million.
That is before the transfer of funds. Those figures represent the actual collections made by the three bodies. The result is that from


1930 to 1951 the municipal revenue had doubled, the provincial revenue had multiplied about six times and the federal revenue had multiplied about 12 times, increasing from $315 million in 1930 to $3,791 million in 1951.
I think we must all agree that this leaves the municipalities in a very difficult situation. The municipal burdens have multiplied and, as has been pointed out, we have the irony that by reason of exceptional activity and tremendous industrial growth the various municipalities which are experiencing this activity in its most extreme form and which are providing huge amounts of taxes for the federal government and are also providing in large measure the gross national product from which the federal government derives buoyant taxes, are having great difficulties in providing their necessary services. If some of the calculations now being made prove to be correct I gather that the federal taxes this year may be so buoyant that the minister's estimate of his surplus may look like small potatoes next December; however, that is in the future, and it is just a matter of gossip.
I suggest that this municipal situation is an urgent problem and that nothing is being done to grapple with it. We are really pretending that it does not exist. I agree with what the minister and someone else said, that even if this resolution were adopted the amounts involved would not go a very great way toward solving the problem; that is why I took great pains to read the broader words which I think are most important:
.	.	. immediate consideration should be given
to measures to assist the municipalities of Canada to meet their mounting financial problems.
I am not fooling myself that those sums will actually make a tremendous difference. What I am interested in is this broad problem of taxing power, to create a situation where those who spend the money shall as far as possible be able to raise it.
I have already tried to say that the things which come from the municipalities are the things of every day importance, things we need and which enter into our lives more closely than anything else. The dominion takes enough money to get along. I can imagine the Minister of Finance saying to a hard-pressed treasurer of a municipality, "How are you getting along? I am all right. I have a nice big surplus." And I can imagine the treasurer of almost any of the thousands of municipalities across Canada saying, "How I envy you; that is not my position." Then he might go on and remind the minister that the reason the minister has this surplus is

because he is taking so much from the citizens of that municipality who usually contribute to him vastly more than they do to their own treasurer.
They might get some back next year.

My colleague has suggested that there might be a method in the minister's attitude. We have already mentioned that, and of course next year is next year with its various possibilities which have not yet been finally declared but upon which we are all reflecting.
I am not going to spend much time in talking about the actual plight of the municipalities. Ottawa has already been referred to, and anyone who drives along the streets of Ottawa must get a terrific object lesson as to what is happening here.
I would like to quote one or two short passages from the remarks made by the premier of Ontario and also the metro chairman. In quoting the premier of Ontario I would like to remind hon. members that he has been a man of moderate statements. I do not think anyone can suggest that moderation is not his characteristic, and when he speaks as strongly as he does I for one feel he is entitled to be taken very seriously indeed. It is not as if someone who has been in the habit of indulging in wild and extreme statements were saying these things; it is quite the contrary.
The other day Mr. Frost felt it necessary to warn the municipalities, and these were his words:
The provinces and its municipalities face the immediate prospect of financial belt-tightening and doing without the roads, sewers and schools and other services which make this province so attractive to industry.
I find that a very disturbing statement. I think we have quite enough knowledge to know it is not an exaggerated statement. I know that two or three years ago the then superintendent of education, Mr. J. G. Althouse, made a comment with regard to the next three years which he described as crucial years. That took place in 1953, and he was right. He was apprehensive of a situation wherein we might not be able to give adequate payment to school teachers. He felt we would have to pay so much for physical things needed in education that we would have to pinch in teachers' salaries which I submit, and I know the minister would agree, is the last place in the world in which we should have to pinch.
At the same time, in speaking of the difficulty of this ironic but real situation, Mr. Gardiner, the metro chairman said:
We have to finance too much expansion in too short a time.
67509-217J
Proposed Tax Relief for Municipalities
Then he went on to explain that the municipalities are poor because of their sudden prosperity. I quote again from Mr. Frost, who in speaking of Ontario's needs said:
They were not imaginary needs and we would not be victims of our own prosperity if we had a realistic share of the tax revenue the producing of which is causing our troubles.
I have taken the people in Ontario to begin with. We are in the midst of great industrial activity which is stimulating a business boom and providing, incidentally a large amount of taxes. I want to refer briefly to Winnipeg, too. An article appeared in the Free Press the other day pointing out the problems the people there are facing. They are looking forward, as is everyone else, to an increase in population. The Free Press had this to say:
Acre upon acre of now undeveloped ground will have to be subdivided, sidewalks and roads will have to be planned, water and sewer lines laid These lines will have to be serviced. A heavier suburban population will complicate traffic to and from the downtown area. This will require new bridges, arterial highways and perimeter roads. There will be many other problems-shopping and industrial districts-parks and schools.
I repeat that I do not believe that anybody looking at the situation as it is thinks the municipalities unaided can take care of this situation for the next few years, and indeed indefinitely into the future. I come back again to what I have said more than once; what I think should happen and what I think is necessary above all things is a frank realization of this and an utter abandonment of the attitude of the Prime Minister, as indicated by the words I quoted a little while ago, when he said he did not see any need to share in the normal cost of the growth of the provinces and the municipalities.
I want to say a word about what has happened elsewhere. In the United States they have roughly the same kind of situation that we have except that there the residue of power is in the state and not with the federal government as in our case. I have here a report which I think is worth putting on the record, although I do dislike reading anything. This is a recommendation to the president's commission on intergovernmental relations in the United States, and I am quoting from section O, page 13 of the brief submitted to the Gordon commission by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities:
The committee recognizes that intergovernmental fiscal relations in a federal system have never been, nor can remain static. A neat allocation of functions to be performed exclusively by each level, a complete separation of revenue sources by levels of government, and a dedication of particular revenue sources to the financing of particular governmental activities-these are no
3418	HOUSE OF

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had been discussing the question raised by the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition. I had confined myself in the main to urging that the broad problem of the mounting costs of municipal administration should be considered, and had said a good deal less about the actual taxes mentioned in the amendment. But the more I think about it the more it seems to me that there is something almost preposterous when one thinks of the situation. Here is the federal government taxing in a good robust way the individuals who are comprised in the municipality. Then when the federal taxpayer has digested the amount of his tax and borne it with as good a grace


as possible, he finds he is attacked from a different direction; that is to say, he is going to be taxed through the municipality to which he belongs. I suggest, as I said a moment ago, that there is something almost preposterous in that.
He pays huge sums to the dominion and then he finds that the municipality to which he has paid his taxes, by reason, as I say, of a situation which I think has reached the impossible, is not able to carry out what he expects it to carry out. I gave an illustration this afternoon, a quotation from Mr. Frost of the restrictions, the drawing in, the retreat which is going to have to be made in the Toronto area, and that is only one of many hundreds of cases across the dominion where no doubt there will be exactly the same kind of difficulty. I suggest that there is bitter irony in it, and that this is something that should be taken seriously.
I am not prepared to offer any facile offhand suggestions as to exactly how the matter should be dealt with. I think it is very difficult. I think it demands great study. But of course the first prerequisite of all is that the government should admit that there is a problem; and as I read twice from the Prime Minister's speech on the address this afternoon the government has clearly announced to us that it apparently does not think there is a problem with which the government should concern itself so far as the municipalities in what is called their "normal" operations are concerned.
Though I am not going to attempt to lay down the detail as to how it should be done, I am going to refer very briefly to a document which contains some very interesting suggestions and which I am sure the minister has seen. It is a document entitled, "Urban Growth and Municipal Finance" prepared by Professor D. C. Corbett of McGill University. I propose to refer very briefly to certain suggestions he makes in the section he has entitled, "The Problem Today", that is, the problem I have been endeavouring to discuss. He says:
What can be done about it? There seem to be two courses open. Either municipalities must be relieved of some of their present responsibilities, and these be taken oyer by senior governments; or the municipalities must find more funds.
There are some who advocate the first approach. They point out that education, health and welfare are national problems, not local ones, and they argue that senior governments should pay for them.
Then he goes on to point out what I think we all recognize, that there are serious dangers in turning over municipal functions to senior governments. It means increased centralization. It means the lessening of a sense of individual responsibility at the stage where it

ought to be strongest, where individual supervision can be most effective. He goes on to say:
The fewer important functions local governments have to perform, the less vital will local democracy be, and the more apathetic will be its electorate and representatives. Strong local governments, doing significant work, are worth preserving . . .
Then he goes on to the second alternative and says:
The second alternative before our municipal governments is finding more revenues. How is this to be done? Some advocate increased provincial grants or even federal grants . . . The scheme is very attractive, has much to recommend it, and under certain conditions may be the proper solution.
But then he raises the objection to that. He says:
A relationship of financial dependency between local and senior governments will inevitably result in increased power for the senior governments.
Much more is said on that but I do not propose to quote it. What I have read raises the points very clearly, and I think we all recognize their importance. Then he goes on to make comments which are especially relevant to what we are considering in this resolution. He says:
. . . there is one form of senior government payment to municipalities which is free from these objections.
That is the objections of centralization and so on. Then he goes on to refer to the payment by senior governments of their municipal taxes on crown property. Later he goes on again to say:
Another way in which the federal and provincial governments could come to the assistance of local governments would be to relieve them from payment of federal or provincially imposed taxes.
He says that a case in point is the federal sales tax. Again I skip. Finally he comes to a point which should not be ignored, and which in itself demands a great deal of study. He says:
The one remaining way to increase municipal revenues is to raise local taxes.
Under that heading he goes on to speak about the real property tax and he says what I think we will all agree with:
But there is no escaping the conclusion that the real property tax has, in genera], failed to keep pace with cost rises and urban growth.
I am not going further into that, Mr. Speaker. I commend this memorandum to the study of everyone who is interested in the problem. I say again that I hope with all my heart the government will abandon the attitude it is taking now, because I believe that here is a very important matter. I believe the analysis of the problem contained in this memorandum goes to the very root of

I should like to say that all the means we have advocated in this house whereby this government might help the lower levels of government, including municipal government, have already been adopted by this Liberal government, and in adopting those measures they have never said that they were violating the spirit of the British North America Act. By the minister's own admission the federal government make funds available for education. They give grants to the universities of Canada. In essence, Mr. Speaker, there is not a particle of difference between giving grants to universities and giving grants to the elementary schools of the nation. Since this government has adopted the principle of some responsibility in some matters in Canada, all we are asking is that they assume sufficient responsibility to enable our lower levels of government to do a job.
In the field of civil defence this government have assumed some responsibility, yet they insist on unloading the major portion of the burden on the lower levels of government. I am not one who for one moment will advocate that this government should assume the entire cost of those functions that are assigned, and wisely so, to the lower levels of government. I think one of the fundamental elements of democracy is that those who administer should also be responsible. In all these measures, therefore, I am advocating only that a larger measure of responsibility for the cost be carried by this government. If we want responsible government, I maintain that those who administer government should be responsible for some share of the cost. However, I feel that at the present time our local governments are asked to assume an undue responsibility when it comes to sharing the cost.
After all in 1867, at the time the fathers of confederation formed Canada, we had an entirely different situation throughout the nation. The major source of revenue to any government at that time was taxation of real estate or taxation of property. At the present time the major sources of revenue are such things as income tax, sales tax, tariffs, duties and so forth. The revenue resources now available were not even visualized or imagined at that time.
In the field of health this government have assumed responsibility. They have never yet said they were violating our constitution when they agreed to pay, in effect, $1,000 per bed as a federal grant for the construction of hospitals. What we complain about is that the lower levels of government which have not had these additional sources of revenue are being asked to pay the remaining $19,000 of the cost of these hospital beds. It simply breaks my heart when I see these

kind, willing and loyal citizens, these ladies of Canada, standing out on the street corners in Canada with their tin cups pleading with you please to buy a tag, or to donate 25 cents to the cancer fund, the heart fund, the Victorian Order of Nurses or what have you.

Yet when it comes to paying a reasonable share in relation to their income, to their share of the national tax dollar, they hide behind the cloak of the British North America Act and say that after all health is a matter for the provincial and municipal governments.

As time goes on we find that more and more of the most valuable downtown properties in our cities are being held by the federal government in order to provide service in one way or another to the public of the city and district served by those particular buildings. That, whereas this municipality contributes in sales tax, annually, an amount totalling approximately $150,000, which is equivalent to one mill in the municipal tax rate;
And whereas it is considered inequitable that the municipality should be required to raise moneys through taxation in order to pay them out again to a senior government in the form of sales tax;

The minister said this afternoon that it had been a principle ever since confederation not to tax the crown. In that statement he admits that the crown may be in the right of the dominion or in the right of the province.

was interested, Mr. Speaker, in the opening observations of the previous speaker, the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary. He suggested that the amendment we have before us was very much the same as material he had presented to the house on an earlier occasion. I believe that only tends to underline the fact that we are facing a real problem, one of the basic problems in Canada, in this matter of municipal tax resources and municipal services.
Ever since I came to this chamber one of the subjects that has been aired repeatedly has been the increasing difficulties that municipalities have in facing their responsibilites in the changing Canadian economy. The problem can be stated very simply, but while the problem can be stated simply unfortunately there is no easy solution. I do feel, however, that it is a difficulty that demands the immediate and earnest attention of government at the federal level. Municipal governments, of course, are very much smaller in their geographic areas and very much restricted when compared with provincial and federal governments. It is for this reason I think we sometimes fail to appreciate the relative importance of the three levels of government.
While it is true that municipal governments seem to be restricted in their authority and the number of people concerned is not too great, I should like to suggest that they are dealing with issues that are of the greatest importance to this country. While as individual units they are small, we must remember that in terms of the over-all national picture we have some 4,000 municipalities and municipal councils; and again

We must not be twisted in our thinking regarding the importance of municipal governments. It has been said today, as it has been many times, that a nation is only as strong as the local level of government. I think it was de Toqueville who said that a nation may establish a system of free government, but without municipal institutions it cannot have the spirit of liberty. It has become a truism to conclude that the real source of democratic government, the real source of liberty, arises on the level of local government. Unless we have a thriving, vital, active local government, we are not going to have a vital democratic government either at provincial or federal levels.
One of the problems of local government today is the great apathy toward responsibility at this level on the part of the individual citizen. Year after year when we come to the time of local elections we are faced with a situation in which it is very difficult to inspire any enthusiasm for the issues at stake. This lack of enthusiasm, this apathy, is indicated by the reluctance of citizens to allow their names to stand for local office. While we sometimes decry the lack of interest in federal elections as represented by the relatively small turnout of voters, certainly the record for both federal and provincial elections is away ahead of the record for local elections. It is not the exception to discover that in municipal elections we have as small a percentage as 35 per cent of the electorate turning out to support a panel of candidates.
This apathy on the local level, I suggest, does not augur very well for the continuing survival of a vital democracy at the higher levels of government. I would further suggest that one of the reasons-there are several reasons-for this failure on the part of citizens to present themselves for service on the local level is the difficult situation confronting municipalities in the changing economic circumstances of the country. The municipality is burdened with services far beyond its capacity to cope with adequately. Anyone who has had any service on the local level of government will realize that life can be one series of problems that are unsolvable; of irate taxpayers waiting on the doorstep and constantly trying to get action; of the local councillor or mayor being only too willing to act but prevented from doing so because of inadequate financial resurces. It is a problem that has to be faced. It is a problem that, while the solution is not easy, certainly a nation such as Canada should endeavour to deal with directly and as quickly as possible.
