As these discussions have illustrated, the federal government attempts to cast off responsibility for the difficulties by referring back to the responsibilities of the provincial government. Unfortunately, in most of the difficulties facing Canada at the moment this tendency for buck-passing has become the chief technique of dealing with problems. The dominion government refers back to the provincial government. If you go to the provincial government they, in turn, say, "Sorry, it is not our responsibility. The federal government will have to deal with this matter." Somebody has to take responsibility for the tax situation that has developed in Canada, particularly since world war II. Certainly the federal government has to take the major responsibility in this regard.
The federal government has moved into the available tax areas to a rapidly expanding extent in recent years. For example, the statistics for 1952 show that the federal government collected $3,792 million; the provincial governments collected $918 million; and the municipal governments, $636 million. The tendency toward centralization of responsibility, largely resulting from the demands of war, is the reason for the pattern indicated by those statistics. Yet notwithstanding those trends the service responsibilities of municipalities have remained largely unchanged; in fact, they have expanded very rapidly in recent years.
It is a well-known fact that those service responsibilities involve the types of government service that have become most expensive in our modern twentieth century civilization; education, health and welfare matters, roads and similar responsibilities. Here again the federal government hides behind the constitutional problem. Admittedly the control of these matters of education, health and welfare and roads has to remain largely in the hands of the local levels of government. That is particularly true of the matter of education, because local control must rest with the municipal governments. The federal government hides behind those constitutional difficulties and professes that nothing can be done by way of sharing responsibility for the increasing financial load.
We have before us an amendment which does not profess to solve the whole difficulty, but it certainly is a gesture in the right direction. Perhaps that is the way we have to move; perhaps this difficulty cannot be solved in one magic wave of the wand. It is a matter of gradual adjustment, a matter of changing circumstances. We have the suggestion that the privileges of exemption from excise and sales taxes might be passed along


to the municipal governments, the same privilege that is also extended to the other level of government, and also the other solution that has been placed before the house.
A few moments ago, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned that the demands in the service areas of education, health and welfare and roads had to remain within the control of local governments, and also that these service demands were expanding very rapidly. The irony of the situation is that the principal reason for the rapid expansion in those service areas has resulted from the actions of the top levels of government provincially, but especially the federal level of government. As Canada moves toward nationhood, as we move into the industrial revolution of the twentieth century, as we move toward a more complex kind of life, the educational facilities, the health and welfare program have to be expanded far beyond the wildest imagination of the founding fathers.
These pressures, as I have indicated, come from the highest level of government, namely the federal government. Today education is a national responsibility. At the time of confederation the financial responsibility for education could be left safely to local levels because it was a matter of reading, writing and arithmetic so the citizenry of a democracy might be able to meet the ordinary demands of communication; but today education has become a terrifically complex and expensive proposition. The matter of national survival is intimately tied up with the kind of educational program we carry on in Canada today. The servicemen serving in the defence of Canada require a relatively high level of general education as well as technical education if Canada is to meet the challenges from any potential aggressor.
In recent days we have heard rather ominous observations to the effect that other nations are away ahead of us in the development of technical skills that would prepare the youth of those nations to play their adequate role in a technological civilization. That is a national responsibility. Certainly it has not very much to do with the local responsibilities which were envisaged at the time education was originally placed in the hands of local government. Then there is the matter of providing education for our new citizens, the immigrants to Canada, which in the post-war years has presented quite a problem to certain communities in which the new Canadians have tended to concentrate. Again this lies within the area of federal responsibility. We are faced with this problem, and maybe there is no absolute solution of it. Education has today moved toward a national perspective, while at the same time

we have to preserve the local responsibilities and the provincial responsibilities under the British North America Act.
I could go on and deal in detail with certain other areas of service responsibilities that fall upon the local levels of government. For example, there is this matter of flooding that we hear about these days, particularly in reference to the perennial difficulties that we have in the province of Manitoba. I attended a meeting of farmers just a couple of weeks ago, a group of farmers and representatives of local municipalities, who have banded themselves together in a voluntary association of municipalities to see whether they cannot come to grips with the question of who is responsible for the control of flood conditions and for looking after the compensation when floods occur.
There the problem was to try to pinpoint where the financial responsibility lay. Provincial authorities say it is with the federal government. Federal authorities say they cannot do anything unless provincial authorities take the initiative. We had another interpretation at this rally, to the effect that if action is required by way of flood control it will be necessary for the local municipalities to approach the authorities and present their case in clear-cut terms. Well, that was a new interpretation, but at least it tended to pinpoint the situation so that some concrete action might be taken.
I listened to the Prime Minister's remarks on this matter when the house opened today, and it seemed to me he was suggesting that this problem of control had become an annual difficulty and that some over-all conservation measures, flood control measures, were urgently required. If we need an overall conservation program I think it is obvious that the municipal and provincial governments cannot be made responsible for it. It seems to me that the federal government must take the initiative for the general wellbeing of Canada, and must deal with matters pertaining to water and soil conservation and the growing problem of flooding which arises from those two difficulties.

For example, the local municipalities no longer have any financial responsibility for providing old age pensions. There is a movement in a more reasonable direction in the light of prevailing conditions in regard to welfare matters. Despite this fact, with the growing pressure from the senior levels of government the municipalities have

I do not think anyone can deny that an adult with a mental age under seven is totally and permanently disabled so far as being an adequately functioning social individual is concerned. When these problems come to the attention of the municipalities they have to assume responsibility, and the pressure has come from action on the part of the senior levels of government.
These matters are well known to all municipal officials, and of course they have been presented in this house on a great many occasions in the past. There is no need to re-emphasize them at great length tonight.

Most

taking responsibility for initiating some positive action to meet this important problem.
Other solutions have been put forward in limited terms in the resolution we have before us, and I refer to the finding of some new tax resources or some new tax techniques which will ease the burden of the local levels of government. Here the possibilities are limited, but we have two simple solutions which have been presented to the house and I am quite happy to support them.
I should like to relate one personal experience in regard to the excise and sales tax situation. Like all municipalities the city of Brandon in recent years has been engaged in extensive public works in the form of the paving of roads, the building of sidewalks and so forth. They had to invest rather heavily in the necessary equipment to carry out this particular work. They obtained the latest type of equipment for the construction of sidewalks and curbs, and were under the impression that as the expenditure was more than $1,000 it would be free from excise and sales taxes. However, they were told that the $1,000 must be considered on a unit basis. The equipment necessary for this particular job did not contain any one unit which involved an expenditure of $1,000. We argued backward and forward with the revenue department for some time, but finally lost because of a regulation which seemed fairly difficult to understand.
The problem which the municipalities are facing may not seem large when measured against the abundant wealth in taxes possessed by the federal government, but when it is measured against the limited revenue of the local government it is large indeed. The total budget for the current year for the city of Brandon is slightly over $1 million. We have the famous phrase, "What is a million dollars?" but the fact is that that is a lot of money to a local municipality. We ran into the same problem in the construction and equipping of a home for senior citizens. There was some technicality which ruled out the remission of the sales and excise taxes because the application had not been made before a particular date.
These may be small things when compared with the total problem represented by the amendment we have before us. As I have indicated, perhaps we will have to move toward the main solution by a series of short steps rather than one panacea which will solve all our difficulties in one stroke.
To bring my remarks to a conclusion, let me say that this problem is felt particularly severely by the rural municipalities. I do not think anyone has spoken today on behalf of

those municipalities. We think of great metropolitan areas like Toronto and Montreal having financial restrictions because of their broad service responsibilities, but in some respects they are better off than the local rural municipalities. The local rural municipality has absolutely no other tax revenue than the tax on real property.
I do not have to draw a diagram in order to point out that our rural municipalities, particularly in western Canada, are not in a very healthy condition. They are financially unsound; they are socially unsound; they are economically unsound. The continuing drift from rural to urban areas has deprived the rural community, which carries an important responsibility in keeping culture and liberty alive, of considerable financial resources. These difficulties represent one of the major problems facing Canada at the present time. I urge the federal government, which does have responsibility in these matters, to give attention to this one.

1.	Has the wheat board given instructions to elevator companies on the prairies that their agents are not to buy wheat produced in the year 1954 or prior thereto?
2.	It so, why were such instructions given?
3.	Do private elevator companies refuse to accept deliveries of wheat produced in the above-mentioned year, or prior thereto?
4.	If so, on what authority?
Answer by: Mr. Dickey, Parliamentary Assistant, for the Minister of Trade and
Commerce:
1.	No.
2.	See answer to No. 1 above.
3.	The receipt of grain into country elevators is subject to the provisions of the Canada Grain Act, which does not distinguish between grain produced in one year and that produced in any other year. Producers' deliveries are, of course, subject to delivery quotas as established from time to time by the Canadian wheat board.
4.	See answer to No. 3 above.
